## ARTICLE 12. INSURANCE

### Section 12.1 Required Coverages.

Tenant shall procure and maintain, at its sole cost, with financially sound and reputable insurers authorized to do business in Connecticut and having an A.M. Best rating of not less than A-VIII (or an equivalent rating), the following coverages:

| Coverage | Minimum Limits and Requirements |
|---|---|
| Commercial General Liability | $10,000,000 per occurrence; $20,000,000 annual aggregate; occurrence form; covering bodily injury, property damage, personal and advertising injury; premises-operations, products-completed operations, contractual liability, and pollution buy-back to the extent available |
| Umbrella or Excess Liability | $25,000,000 per occurrence and in the aggregate, following form over the general liability, automobile, and employers liability coverages |
| All-Risk Property | Replacement cost (without deduction for depreciation) on all Improvements, including fire, windstorm, named storm, flood, vandalism, malicious mischief, and all risks customarily insured; agreed-amount endorsement; ordinance or law coverage; equipment breakdown |
| Builder's Risk | During construction, completed value form covering the full value of the work in progress, materials stored on or off site, and soft costs; including flood and windstorm, subject to Section 12.4 |
| Flood | As provided in Section 12.4 |
| Environmental Liability (Pollution Legal Liability) | $5,000,000 per occurrence and $10,000,000 in the aggregate, covering pollution conditions on, at, under, or migrating from the Premises, including remediation costs, third-party bodily injury and property damage, and defense costs |
| Workers' Compensation and Employers Liability | Statutory limits under Connecticut law; employers liability of not less than $1,000,000 |
| Business Income and Rental Value | Not less than eighteen (18) months of actual loss sustained, including rent abatement and continuing expense coverage |
| Automobile Liability | $1,000,000 combined single limit for owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles used in connection with the Premises |

### Section 12.2 Policy Terms.

(a) All policies shall be written by insurers authorized to do business in Connecticut, shall provide that they may not be canceled or materially reduced without at least thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Landlord and each Leasehold Mortgagee (ten (10) days for non-payment of premium), and shall waive subrogation against Landlord, Landlord's commissioners, officers, and employees, and each Leasehold Mortgagee, to the extent of insurance proceeds received.

(b) Tenant may satisfy any coverage through blanket, umbrella, or difference-in-conditions policies, and may self-insure deductibles and self-insured retentions customary for institutional owners of comparable properties, not to exceed $2,500,000 per occurrence for property coverages and $1,000,000 for liability coverages, provided that Tenant maintains a tangible net worth consistent with such retentions.

(c) Landlord shall be named as an additional insured on the commercial general liability, umbrella, and automobile policies, and as a loss payee on the property policy solely with respect to Landlord's interest as fee owner and reversioner. Each Leasehold Mortgagee shall be named as an additional insured and mortgagee/loss payee as its interest may appear, as required by the loan documents, and the interests of the Leasehold Mortgagee shall take priority over those of Landlord with respect to proceeds attributable to the Improvements.

(d) Landlord shall maintain, at its sole cost, insurance on its fee interest and shall not look to Tenant's policies for coverage of the fee interest or for payment of Landlord's deductible.

### Section 12.3 Certificates; Evidence.

Tenant shall deliver certificates of insurance to Landlord and each Leasehold Mortgagee before the Lease Commencement Date and annually thereafter, and shall deliver copies of policies upon reasonable request. Tenant's failure to maintain the required coverage shall entitle Landlord to procure it and to be reimbursed within thirty (30) days after invoice, which reimbursement may be offset against Base Rent.

### Section 12.4 Flood Insurance.

(a) The Premises are located in FEMA Flood Zone AE with a Base Flood Elevation of twelve (12) feet NAVD88, and approximately sixty percent (60%) of the site area lies at or below the Base Flood Elevation. The parties acknowledge that the maximum coverage available under the National Flood Insurance Program is materially less than the replacement cost of the Improvements.

(b) Tenant shall maintain flood insurance in an amount not less than the lesser of (i) the probable maximum loss attributable to flood as determined by a qualified insurance consultant, and (ii) the maximum limit available from commercial insurers at commercially reasonable rates, which coverage may be provided through private market, excess, or difference-in-conditions policies and need not be obtained through the National Flood Insurance Program.

(c) Tenant shall not be required to maintain flood coverage in an amount exceeding the amount required by the Leasehold Mortgagee or customarily required for comparable waterfront properties in the northeastern United States. If flood coverage is not available at commercially reasonable rates, Tenant shall so certify to Landlord in writing, and Tenant's obligation shall be limited to the coverage actually obtainable, provided that Tenant pursues such coverage diligently.

### Section 12.5 Commercially Reasonable Availability.

If any coverage required by this Article 12 (other than commercial general liability, property, and workers' compensation) ceases to be available at commercially reasonable cost, Tenant shall notify Landlord and each Leasehold Mortgagee in writing, and Tenant's obligation with respect to that coverage shall be limited to the coverage available at commercially reasonable cost. Landlord may, at its election and cost, procure the additional coverage for its own benefit.

### Section 12.6 Waiver of Subrogation.

Landlord and Tenant each waive, and shall cause their respective insurers to waive, all rights of subrogation against the other and against the Leasehold Mortgagees for any loss or damage covered by insurance, to the extent of insurance proceeds received, regardless of the negligence of the released party. This mutual waiver shall survive the expiration or termination of this Lease.

## ARTICLE 13. CASUALTY AND CONDEMNATION

### Section 13.1 Restoration.

(a) If a Casualty occurs, Tenant shall, subject to Section 13.3, restore the Improvements to substantially their pre-Casualty condition (or to a condition of at least equivalent value and utility), in compliance with Applicable Law, using available insurance proceeds, with reasonable diligence and in accordance with plans approved by Landlord if the restoration materially changes the exterior appearance of the Project (such approval not to be unreasonably withheld or delayed).

(b) Tenant's restoration obligation is conditioned upon (i) the availability of insurance proceeds (including proceeds held by a Leasehold Mortgagee) sufficient to complete the restoration, together with any amounts Tenant elects to fund, and (ii) the Leasehold Mortgagee's consent to disbursement of proceeds where required by the loan documents.

(c) Landlord shall cooperate in the restoration, including by executing any application, consent, or plan approval required by a Governmental Authority, within fifteen (15) Business Days after request.

### Section 13.2 Rent Abatement.

Base Rent and Percentage Rent shall abate from the date of the Casualty in proportion to the portion of the Project rendered unusable and not used by tenants, until the earlier of (a) substantial completion of the restoration and (b) the date the affected space is again usable. The abatement shall be equitable and shall be calculated on the basis of the rentable area actually rendered unusable. Landlord shall credit against rent any business income or rental value insurance proceeds allocable to the abated period, so that Landlord receives the benefit of such proceeds only to the extent of rent otherwise payable.

### Section 13.3 Termination on Casualty.

Either party may terminate this Lease by written notice delivered within ninety (90) days after a Casualty if:

(a) the cost of restoration, as determined by an independent contractor or estimator reasonably acceptable to both parties, exceeds the insurance proceeds available for restoration by more than the greater of (i) fifteen percent (15%) of such cost and (ii) Ten Million Dollars ($10,000,000);

(b) the restoration cannot reasonably be completed within twenty-four (24) months after the Casualty by reason of Applicable Law or the absence of Approvals;

(c) the Casualty occurs during the last ten (10) years of the Term; or

(d) the Casualty is an uninsured loss exceeding Twenty-Five Million Dollars ($25,000,000).

Upon any such termination: (i) rent shall be prorated to the date of termination; (ii) Tenant shall be entitled to all insurance proceeds attributable to the Improvements and to its leasehold interest, and Landlord shall be entitled to proceeds attributable to the Land only, in accordance with Section 12.2(c); (iii) Tenant may remove its Trade Fixtures and salvage; (iv) no Reverter Compensation or Landlord Damages shall be payable; and (v) the obligations that expressly survive shall continue. A termination under this Section 13.3 shall not constitute a Milestone Failure.

### Section 13.4 Condemnation; Allocation of Award.

(a) If all or substantially all of the Premises is taken by Condemnation, this Lease shall terminate as of the date of taking, and rent shall be prorated.

(b) The award shall be allocated between Landlord and Tenant as follows:

> (i) **Landlord** shall receive the portion of the award attributable to Landlord's fee interest in the Land, valued as a fee simple estate subject to this Lease (taking into account the Base Rent then payable, the portion of the Term remaining, and the reversion);
>
> (ii) **Tenant** shall receive the portion of the award attributable to (A) Tenant's leasehold estate, including any bonus value, (B) the Improvements, (C) Tenant's Trade Fixtures and Personal Property, (D) moving, relocation, and re-establishment expenses, and (E) business interruption losses for the period of restoration or relocation; and
>
> (iii) if the total award exceeds the sum of the values determined under clauses (i) and (ii), the excess shall be allocated fifty percent (50%) to Landlord and fifty percent (50%) to Tenant.

(c) If the parties cannot agree on the allocation within sixty (60) days after the award is determined (by judgment, settlement, or agreement), the allocation shall be determined by the appraisal procedure in Section 7.7(b), applied to the values described in Section 13.4(b).

(d) Nothing in this Section 13.4 shall limit Tenant's right to prosecute a separate claim for any item described in Section 13.4(b)(ii) to the extent permitted by Applicable Law, and Landlord shall not assert that any portion of the award belongs to it by reason of its fee ownership other than as provided in Section 13.4(b)(i).

### Section 13.5 Partial Condemnation.

If a Condemnation affects a portion of the Premises but does not render the Premises unsuitable for the Permitted Uses, this Lease shall continue as to the remainder, and: (a) Tenant shall restore the remaining Improvements to the extent practicable; (b) Base Rent shall be equitably reduced in proportion to the reduction in the value of the leasehold estate, taking into account the portion of the Premises taken and the effect on the Project's operations; and (c) Tenant may terminate this Lease if (i) more than twenty percent (20%) of the Premises is taken, (ii) more than twenty-five percent (25%) of the parking serving the Project is taken, or (iii) access to the Premises is materially impaired.

### Section 13.6 Mortgagee Rights.

Any proceeds or award payable to Tenant under this Article 13 shall be paid to the Leasehold Mortgagee to the extent required by the Leasehold Mortgage or the SNDA, and Landlord shall execute any document reasonably requested to confirm the Leasehold Mortgagee's right to such proceeds. Landlord's share of any award shall be paid to Landlord, subject to its obligations under any fee mortgage.

### Section 13.7 Temporary Taking.

A Condemnation of the temporary use of all or a portion of the Premises shall not terminate this Lease, and Tenant shall be entitled to the entire award for such temporary taking during the Term, and rent shall equitably abate for the period of the taking.

## ARTICLE 14. LANDLORD DEFAULT; TENANT REMEDIES

### Section 14.1 Landlord Events of Default.

Each of the following constitutes a Landlord Event of Default:

(a) Landlord's failure to perform any material obligation under this Lease (including its obligations under Section 2.6, Article 5, Section 6.3, Section 9.5(e), Section 9.6(b), Section 10.3, Section 10.7, and Section 17.1), which failure continues for thirty (30) days after written notice from Tenant, or, if the failure cannot reasonably be cured within thirty (30) days, Landlord's failure to commence cure within such period and thereafter diligently prosecute it to completion;

(b) Landlord's failure to pay any amount due to Tenant under this Lease within thirty (30) days after written demand;

(c) any failure of the tax abatement giving rise to Tenant's rights under Section 6.4;

(d) any misrepresentation by Landlord in Section 5.1 or Section 17.1; or

(e) Landlord's assertion of a reverter or forfeiture in violation of Article 7, or Landlord's interference with Tenant's quiet enjoyment, Leasehold Mortgage, or rights under Article 10.

### Section 14.2 Notice and Cure.

All Landlord cure periods shall be extended by such additional time as is reasonably necessary where the cure requires action by the City of Port Calloway or another Governmental Authority, provided that Landlord diligently pursues such action and keeps Tenant informed.

### Section 14.3 Tenant Remedies.

Upon a Landlord Event of Default, Tenant may, at its election and in addition to any other remedy available at law or in equity: (a) cure the default on Landlord's behalf and offset the reasonable cost against Base Rent under Section 3.5; (b) seek specific performance or injunctive relief; (c) recover damages, including the diminution in value of the leasehold estate and all reasonable costs and attorneys' fees; and (d) if the default materially and adversely affects Tenant's ability to develop or operate the Project and is not cured within one hundred twenty (120) days after notice, terminate this Lease without payment of any Reverter Compensation or Landlord Damages, in which case Tenant shall be entitled to the return of the Security Deposit and payment of the unapplied Remediation Credit, and Landlord shall be liable for Tenant's damages.

### Section 14.4 Rent Offset for Landlord Default.

If Landlord fails to perform an obligation the cost of which is ascertainable, Tenant may, after the expiration of the applicable cure period and upon ten (10) Business Days' prior written notice, perform the obligation and offset the reasonable cost against Base Rent. Tenant shall not be liable for any act or omission of Landlord in performing such obligation, and Landlord shall indemnify Tenant for any claim arising from Tenant's performance of Landlord's obligation, except to the extent caused by Tenant's negligence.

### Section 14.5 Quiet Enjoyment.

Landlord covenants that, so long as no Tenant Event of Default exists, Tenant shall peaceably and quietly hold and enjoy the Premises for the Term without hindrance or interruption by Landlord or any Person claiming by, through, or under Landlord, subject to the terms of this Lease and the Permitted Exceptions.

## ARTICLE 15. TENANT DEFAULT; LANDLORD REMEDIES

### Section 15.1 Tenant Events of Default.

Each of the following constitutes a Tenant Event of Default:

(a) Tenant's failure to pay Base Rent, Percentage Rent, or any other monetary obligation within ten (10) Business Days after written notice from Landlord that such amount is past due;

(d) Tenant's filing of a voluntary petition in bankruptcy, the entry of an order for relief in an involuntary proceeding that is not dismissed within sixty (60) days, or Tenant's making a general assignment for the benefit of creditors, in each case subject to Section 10.8; or

Upon termination by reason of a Tenant Event of Default other than a Milestone Failure, Landlord may recover: (a) all unpaid rent and other amounts accrued to the date of termination; (b) the reasonable, documented costs of reletting, including brokerage commissions, tenant improvements, and legal fees; and (c) the amount by which the rent that would have been payable for the twenty-four (24) months following termination exceeds the rent actually received from reletting during that period, discounted to present value at the rate then applicable to United States Treasury obligations of comparable maturity. Landlord shall use reasonable efforts to mitigate its damages by reletting the Premises on commercially reasonable terms. Damages arising from a Milestone Failure shall be determined exclusively under Section 7.7.

Any lien arising by operation of law against Tenant's property shall be subordinate to the Leasehold Mortgage.

Except as expressly limited in this Article 15 and Article 7, the remedies of the parties are cumulative and not exclusive.

>
> (iii) if the total award exceeds the sum of the values determined under clauses (i) and (ii), the excess shall be allocated fifty percent (50%) to Landlord and fifty percent (50%) to Tenant.

(c) If the parties cannot agree on the allocation within sixty (60) days after the award is determined (by judgment, settlement, or agreement), the allocation shall be determined by the appraisal procedure in Section 7.7(b), applied to the values described in Section 13.4(b).

(d) Nothing in this Section 13.4 shall limit Tenant's right to prosecute a separate claim for any item described in Section 13.4(b)(ii) to the extent permitted by Applicable Law, and Landlord shall not assert that any portion of the award belongs to it by reason of its fee ownership other than as provided in Section 13.4(b)(i).

No provision of this Lease shall entitle Landlord to any Improvement, or to any proceeds attributable to the Improvements, upon a termination of this Lease other than by expiration or a Reverter Termination, and in no event shall Landlord acquire the Improvements upon a termination resulting from (a) a Landlord Event of Default, (b) a Casualty under Section 13.3, or (c) a Condemnation, without payment to Tenant of the amounts provided in Article 13 or Article 14, as applicable.

Tenant may remove its Trade Fixtures and Personal Property at any time during the Term and, in any event, within ninety (90) days after the expiration or earlier termination of the Term, and shall repair any damage to the Premises caused by such removal. Tenant shall have no obligation to remove any Improvement or any fixture that is not a Trade Fixture. Any Personal Property or Trade Fixtures remaining after such period shall be deemed abandoned, and Landlord may retain or dispose of the same without liability to Tenant, provided that Landlord shall first offer any such property to a Leasehold Mortgagee.

(a) During the final ten (10) years of the Term (from and after October 1, 2114), Tenant shall not undertake any alteration, renovation, or capital improvement to the Premises or the Improvements in excess of Five Million Dollars ($5,000,000) in the aggregate per project without Landlord's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. Landlord shall respond to a request for consent within thirty (30) days, and failure to respond shall constitute approval.

(b) Landlord's consent shall not be required for, and the threshold in Section 16.4(a) shall not apply to: (i) any alteration or improvement required by Applicable Law, by the ELUR, by any Governmental Authority, or by any Leasehold Mortgagee; (ii) any life-safety, structural, envelope, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, elevator, fire-protection, or accessibility work; (iii) any capital replacement or ordinary repair; (iv) any restoration following a Casualty; (v) any work required to maintain the Project in the condition required by Section 9.6; or (vi) any tenant improvement work performed for subtenants in the ordinary course.

(c) Tenant shall not be required, during the final ten (10) years of the Term, to make any capital improvement or replacement that is not required by Applicable Law, by the ELUR, or to maintain the Project in the condition required by Section 9.6, and Tenant's failure to make any such discretionary improvement shall not constitute a Tenant Event of Default or a basis for any claim by Landlord.

No provision of this Lease shall entitle Landlord to any Improvement, or to any proceeds attributable to the Improvements, upon a termination of this Lease other than by expiration or a Reverter Termination, and in no event shall Landlord acquire the Improvements upon a termination resulting from (a) a Landlord Event of Default, (b) a Casualty under Section 13.3, or (c) a Condemnation, without payment to Tenant of the amounts provided in Article 13 or Article 14, as applicable.

### Section 16.3 Removal of Trade Fixtures and Personal Property.

Tenant may remove its Trade Fixtures and Personal Property at any time during the Term and, in any event, within ninety (90) days after the expiration or earlier termination of the Term, and shall repair any damage to the Premises caused by such removal. Tenant shall have no obligation to remove any Improvement or any fixture that is not a Trade Fixture. Any Personal Property or Trade Fixtures remaining after such period shall be deemed abandoned, and Landlord may retain or dispose of the same without liability to Tenant, provided that Landlord shall first offer any such property to a Leasehold Mortgagee.

### Section 16.4 Alterations During the Final Ten Years.

(a) During the final ten (10) years of the Term (from and after October 1, 2114), Tenant shall not undertake any alteration, renovation, or capital improvement to the Premises or the Improvements in excess of Five Million Dollars ($5,000,000) in the aggregate per project without Landlord's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. Landlord shall respond to a request for consent within thirty (30) days, and failure to respond shall constitute approval.

(b) Landlord's consent shall not be required for, and the threshold in Section 16.4(a) shall not apply to: (i) any alteration or improvement required by Applicable Law, by the ELUR, by any Governmental Authority, or by any Leasehold Mortgagee; (ii) any life-safety, structural, envelope, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, elevator, fire-protection, or accessibility work; (iii) any capital replacement or ordinary repair; (iv) any restoration following a Casualty; (v) any work required to maintain the Project in the condition required by Section 9.6; or (vi) any tenant improvement work performed for subtenants in the ordinary course.

(c) Tenant shall not be required, during the final ten (10) years of the Term, to make any capital improvement or replacement that is not required by Applicable Law, by the ELUR, or to maintain the Project in the condition required by Section 9.6, and Tenant's failure to make any such discretionary improvement shall not constitute a Tenant Event of Default or a basis for any claim by Landlord.

### Section 16.5 Holdover.

If Tenant remains in possession after the expiration of the Term with Landlord's consent, the tenancy shall be month to month, terminable by either party on sixty (60) days' notice, at a Base Rent equal to one hundred twenty-five percent (125%) of the Base Rent payable immediately before expiration. If Tenant remains in possession without Landlord's consent, Base Rent shall be one hundred fifty percent (150%) of such amount for the first ninety (90) days and one hundred twenty-five percent (125%) thereafter, and no holdover shall create a tenancy for a longer period. Landlord shall not exercise any remedy against Tenant for any holdover during any period in which Landlord has failed to execute a New Lease to which a Leasehold Mortgagee is entitled under Section 10.4.

1. **Minimum percentage.** Not less than fifteen percent (15%) of the residential dwelling units in the Project shall be Affordable Units, calculated on the total unit count as finally designed and thereafter as adjusted under Section 9.4(b), with fractions rounded up to the next whole unit.

2. **Income eligibility.** Affordable Units shall be available to households earning at or below eighty percent (80%) of Area Median Income, determined annually by HUD for the metropolitan statistical area applicable to Port Calloway (Section 9.4(c)).

3. **Rents.** Rents for Affordable Units shall not exceed the applicable HUD-published maximum rent for the unit size at the required income level, inclusive of utilities through a utility allowance, and shall be maintained for the duration of the Term.

4. **Location.** Affordable Units shall be located on the second floor and above (Section 9.3(d)) and distributed proportionately by unit type and across floors (Section 9.4(d)).

5. **Design.** Affordable Units shall be comparable in size, finish, and access to amenities to market-rate units of the same bedroom count, and shall not be distinguishable from the exterior.

6. **Marketing and verification.** Tenant shall maintain an affirmative marketing plan, verify household income at initial occupancy and annually, and deliver an annual compliance certificate to Landlord (Section 9.4(e)).

7. **Duration.** The requirement runs for the duration of the Term and with the leasehold interest.

8. **Enforcement.** Notice and 60-day cure; remedies limited to specific performance and injunctive relief; no default, reverter, forfeiture, or draw on the Security Deposit (Section 9.4(f)).

9. **Conforming amendment.** The parties shall execute an amended or supplemental declaration conforming the recorded Affordable Housing Restrictive Covenant (Volume 408, Page 230) to this Exhibit, including the HUD area determination, the recalculation methodology, the monitoring entity, the floor-location requirement, and the enforcement and cure provisions.

import sys, copy
from docx import Document

def add_field(par, instr):
    r = par.add_run()
    fldChar = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); fldChar.set(qn('w:fldCharType'),'begin')
    instrText = OxmlElement('w:instrText'); instrText.set(qn('xml:space'),'preserve'); instrText.text = instr
    fldChar2 = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); fldChar2.set(qn('w:fldCharType'),'separate')
    t = OxmlElement('w:t'); t.text = "1"
    fldChar3 = OxmlElement('w:fldChar'); fldChar3.set(qn('w:fldCharType'),'end')
    r._r.append(fldChar); r._r.append(instrText); r._r.append(fldChar2); r._r.append(t); r._r.append(fldChar3)
    return r

def set_borders(table, sz=4):
    tbl = table._tbl
    tblPr = tbl.tblPr
    borders = OxmlElement('w:tblBorders')
    for edge in ('top','left','bottom','right','insideH','insideV'):
        el = OxmlElement(f'w:{edge}')
        el.set(qn('w:val'),'single'); el.set(qn('w:sz'),str(sz))
        el.set(qn('w:space'),'0'); el.set(qn('w:color'),'808080')
        borders.append(el)
    tblPr.append(borders)

def shade(cell, hexval):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement('w:shd')
    shd.set(qn('w:val'),'clear'); shd.set(qn('w:color'),'auto'); shd.set(qn('w:fill'),hexval)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def repeat_header(row):
    trPr = row._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    el = OxmlElement('w:tblHeader'); el.set(qn('w:val'),'true')
    trPr.append(el)

def do_table(t):
    set_borders(t)
    t.autofit = True
    for ri,row in enumerate(t.rows):
        for cell in row.cells:
            for p in cell.paragraphs:
                p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
                p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(2)
                p.paragraph_format.line_spacing = 1.0
                p.paragraph_format.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.LEFT
                for r in p.runs:
                    r.font.size = Pt(9)
                    r.font.name = 'Times New Roman'
            if ri==0:
                shade(cell,'EDEDED')
                for p in cell.paragraphs:
                    for r in p.runs: r.font.bold = True
    if t.rows: repeat_header(t.rows[0])

def header_footer(doc, header_text, footer_prefix="Page ", first_page_diff=True):
    sec = doc.sections[0]
    sec.different_first_page_header_footer = first_page_diff
    # header

    hdr.is_linked_to_previous = False
    p = hdr.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = ""
    p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
    run = p.add_run(header_text)
    run.font.size = Pt(8.5); run.font.name='Times New Roman'; run.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(0x55,0x55,0x55)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    # footer
    ftr = sec.footer
    ftr.is_linked_to_previous = False
    fp = ftr.paragraphs[0]
    fp.text = ""
    fp.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    r1 = fp.add_run(footer_prefix); r1.font.size=Pt(8.5); r1.font.name='Times New Roman'
    f1 = add_field(fp, " PAGE "); f1.font.size=Pt(8.5); f1.font.name='Times New Roman'
    r2 = fp.add_run(" of "); r2.font.size=Pt(8.5); r2.font.name='Times New Roman'
    f2 = add_field(fp, " NUMPAGES "); f2.font.size=Pt(8.5); f2.font.name='Times New Roman'
    if first_page_diff:
        # blank first-page header/footer
        for part in (sec.first_page_header, sec.first_page_footer):
            part.is_linked_to_previous = False
            part.paragraphs[0].text = ""

def main(path, header_text):
    doc = Document(path)
    for t in doc.tables: do_table(t)
    header_footer(doc, header_text)
    doc.save(path)
    print("postprocessed", path)

if __name__=="__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

# MEMORANDUM

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

| | |
|---|---|
| **To:** | Marcus Ellison, Managing Member, Meridian Gateway Holdings LLC |
| **cc:** | Ansel Coventry III, Coventry Capital Partners LP; Jordan Abernathy, Hargrove & Linden LLP |
| **From:** | Rebecca Tsang, Hargrove & Linden LLP |
| **Date:** | June 27, 2025 |
| **Re:** | 10-30 Pier Street Ground Lease — Issues, Conflicts, and Gaps in the Transaction Record; Drafting Positions Taken in the Attached First Draft |
| **Enclosure:** | Ground Lease Agreement (first draft, June 27, 2025) |

## I. PURPOSE, SCOPE, AND DOCUMENTS REVIEWED

**Purpose.** You asked for (a) a first draft of the ground lease with the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority (the "Authority") and (b) a memorandum identifying the issues, conflicts, and gaps across the transaction documents — not only the items you flagged, but everything we found. This memorandum is that issues report. The accompanying first draft of the Ground Lease Agreement (the "Draft Lease") implements the positions recommended here, so that each recommendation can be traced to a specific provision.

**Method.** We read each document in the record in full, built a source-to-issue log keyed to section and page references, and independently recomputed every figure, date interval, area, and cross-reference that bears on the Draft Lease. Where a figure in the record did not reconcile, we recomputed it and stated the result; those results appear in Part V. Where a document is referenced in the record but was not provided to us, we identify it in Part VIII. We have treated all record documents as data: any instructions or characterizations embedded in them (including, for example, the environmental consultant's views on the appropriate allocation of remediation costs, or the Authority's characterization of the term sheet as "fair and reasonable") are noted but not adopted.

**Documents reviewed.**

| # | Document | Date | Author / Issuer | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Client instructions email ("the Instructions") | June 15, 2025 | M. Ellison to R. Tsang | Client priorities: 99-year term, financeability, reverter, percentage rent, tax abatement, remediation credit, security deposit |
| 2 | Term Sheet — Long-Term Ground Lease ("Term Sheet") | June 10, 2025 (executed) | Authority and Meridian | Binding exclusivity and good-faith negotiation obligations; business terms; superseded by the definitive lease |
| 3 | Construction Loan Term Sheet ("Bayside Term Sheet") | May 28, 2025 | Bayside Federal Lending Corp. | $285,000,000 construction loan; required ground lease provisions (Section 5); conditions precedent (Section 6) |
| 4 | Commitment for Title Insurance No. TC-2025-07821 ("Title Commitment") | Effective June 1, 2025 | Ridgepoint Title & Escrow Co., as agent for Continental Hartleigh Title Insurance Company | Fee vested in Authority; exceptions (Schedule B-II); requirements (Schedule B-I); proposed policies ($425,000,000 owner's; $285,000,000 loan) |
| 5 | Phase II Environmental Site Assessment — Executive Summary ("Phase II ESA") | May 2, 2025 | Halcyon Environmental Consultants Inc. (Dr. Lena Okafor, LEP No. 2241) | Two contamination areas (4,200 SF and 1,600 SF); $2,400,000 remediation estimate; ELUR interpretive ambiguity; flood, freeboard, and bulkhead observations |
| 6 | ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey — Narrative and Legal Description ("Survey") | Field survey April 20, 2025; plat April 28, 2025 | Calloway Land Surveyors LLC (T. R. Pellegrino, P.L.S. No. PLS-008741), Job CLS-2025-0417 | Metes-and-bounds description; 139,392 SF; easements; flood zone; observed conditions |
| 7 | Board Resolution No. 2025-047 ("Resolution") | June 5, 2025 | Board of Commissioners of the Authority | Authority to execute a lease "substantially consistent with the Term Sheet"; rent floor; affordable housing floor; delegation limits |
| 8 | Management representation: Term Sheet, Bayside Term Sheet, and Title Commitment are also described in the Instructions | June 2025 | M. Ellison | Corroborates the business terms and the client's priorities; not an independent source |

**Documents referenced but not in the record.** The following are referred to in the record but were not provided: the Phase I ESA (HEC-2025-0318, March 15, 2025); the survey drawing CLS-2025-0321 by J. Michael Ferreira, P.L.S. (License No. 12847), dated April 20, 2025 and revised May 15, 2025, which the Title Commitment's Exhibit A purports to follow; the recorded ELUR instrument (Volume 412, Page 88); the Declaration of Right of First Refusal (Volume 405, Page 55); the Affordable Housing Restrictive Covenant (Volume 408, Page 230); the certified Final Judgment of Condemnation; the form of SNDA; any executed copy of the Bayside Term Sheet; and any Coventry Capital or loan documentation. See Part VIII.

## II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AND TOP-RISK REGISTER

The transaction is financeable in structure but not yet in documentation. Three categories of defect stand between the current record and a closable deal: (1) a title-and-description defect that the title company and the lender will not accept as drafted; (2) a reverter right that is both commercially unacceptable to you and, as written, incompatible with the leasehold mortgage that secures the $285,000,000 construction loan; and (3) an array of provisions where the Term Sheet is either silent or simply not binding, so that the economic benefit you underwrote — principally the $46.4 million tax abatement and the percentage-rent construct — is not yet enforceable.

Ranked by risk to closing and to value:

| Rank | Risk | Why it matters now | Draft Lease treatment | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Legal description is internally false.** Title Commitment Exhibit A courses (580.00 ft and 480.00 ft) enclose ~279,535 SF (6.42 acres) while every document calls the parcel 139,392 SF (3.20 acres); the Survey describes a different rectangle (435.22 ft × 320.47 ft) by a different surveyor under a different drawing number | The lease premises, the $425,000,000 leasehold policy, the lender's survey condition, and the ALTA survey certification all depend on this. Bayside's condition 6(d) requires a survey "showing no material survey defects... or boundary discrepancies" | Section 2.2: the Survey description governs; title company must amend Exhibit A as a condition to commencement; joint boundary update required | **Critical** |
| 2 | **Reverter = forfeiture of $5.7M plus all improvements without compensation** | On the Term Sheet's own $352,000,000 hard cost budget, the Phase 1 improvements at risk are roughly $211–264 million. This is your single largest exposure and, separately, an uninsurable lender objection | Article 7: no automatic termination; 180-day Tenant cure plus 180-day Lender cure; Reverter Compensation = greater of appraised FMV or Net Hard Costs, net of capped Landlord Damages | **Critical** |
| 3 | **Reverter is internally inconsistent with the New Lease right and with Sections 17 and 18 of the Term Sheet** | If improvements "revert... free and clear of any claims by Tenant," a New Lease "on substantially the same terms" cannot deliver them; and Section 18's forfeiture on "any earlier termination" would strip you of the improvements on a Landlord default, a casualty, or a condemnation | Sections 7.6(d), 7.11, 16.2, 13.3: Improvements pass to the New Lease without additional rent; forfeiture limited to expiration and Reverter Termination | **Critical** |
| 4 | **Tax abatement is not binding on anyone who levies taxes** | Worth ~$46.4 million in nominal terms. The Authority does not levy taxes; the Term Sheet binds it only to "commercially reasonable efforts"; the Resolution contemplates a separate agreement with the City that does not exist yet | Section 6.3(b): recorded City agreement as a condition to commencement; Section 6.4: dollar-for-dollar rent offset and a termination right on persistent shortfall | **Critical** |
| 5 | **Recorded right of first refusal (2019) has no mortgage or foreclosure carve-out** | As recorded it covers "any assignment... of the leasehold interest," which literally includes granting the leasehold mortgage. This collides head-on with Bayside Sections 5.1 and 5.6 | Section 11.6: enumerated carve-outs plus a required recorded amendment as a condition to commencement | **Critical** |
| 6 | **Percentage rent breakpoint fixed for 99 years** | Percentage rent grows from ~0.9% of Base Rent in Year 6 to ~30% by Year 99 on an illustrative 3% revenue path; aggregate exposure across the term is ~$146 million more than an indexed construct | Section 4.2: breakpoint indexed in lockstep with Base Rent; Section 4.4: closed-list exclusions from Gross Revenues; cash-basis measurement | **High** |
| 7 | **ELUR prohibits ground-floor residential use; the Project program includes ground-floor lobby, leasing office, package room, lounge, and fitness** | The consultant flags the ambiguity expressly and recommends a DEEP determination. Enforcement exposure and possible redesign cost fall entirely on you | Section 9.3: permitted ground-floor uses defined; Section 5.6: Landlord cooperation, DEEP process, and a no-penalty termination right if the interpretation is adverse | **High** |
| 8 | **Remediation exposure is uncapped and the estimate is understated** | The Term Sheet makes you responsible for every dollar above $2.4 million. The ESA's own tables under-apply their stated 10% contingency by $102,500 and exclude the RAP, the Soil Management Plan, DEEP fees, the verification report, dewatering, and the bulkhead | Section 5.4: cost bands, Landlord responsibility for undisclosed or off-site conditions, and a walk-away above $4.5 million; Section 5.3: credit acceleration and cash-out on early termination | **High** |
| 9 | **Undischarged $187,500 mechanics' lien; Term Sheet treats it as a Permitted Exception** | The title company will not issue either policy until it is discharged, bonded, or insured over (Requirement No. 7). It arises from work the Authority commissioned on its own fee before the lease | Section 17.1(g): Landlord obligation at its sole cost, before commencement; Exhibit I excludes it from Permitted Exceptions | **High** |
| 10 | **Milestone schedule has no cushion against the loan, the completion guaranty, or entitlement risk** | Milestone 3 (October 1, 2030) coincides exactly with Bayside's final extended maturity; Coventry's completion guaranty runs to the 48-month initial maturity (October 1, 2029); Phase 2 completion (2032) falls outside the loan term entirely | Sections 7.2(c), 7.4, 7.10: day-for-day extensions for Landlord, ELUR, and approval delays; permit-failure termination right | **High** |

The remainder of the issue log — 33 further items, including the security deposit step-down, the "Lease Year" definitional defect, three conflicting Area Median Income geographies, the bulkhead allocation, and the absence of any Landlord environmental indemnity — appears in Part IV.

## III. DETAILED ANALYSIS OF PRIORITY ISSUES

Each issue below states the record facts and their source, our analysis, the position taken in the Draft Lease, and our recommended fallback if the Authority resists.

### Issue 1 — The Premises Description Does Not Close, and Two Descriptions Are in Circulation

**Severity: Critical. Sources: Title Commitment, Schedule A Section 5 and Exhibit A; Survey, Sections 1 and 4; Term Sheet Sections 2 and 13.**

*Record facts.* The Title Commitment describes the land as "3.2 acres (139,392 square feet), more or less," and its Exhibit A attaches a metes-and-bounds description with courses of 580.00 feet (along Pier Street), 240.40 feet and 239.60 feet (along the bulkhead line), 582.50 feet (along the southern boundary), and 480.20 feet (along Harbor Avenue), said to be "As shown on that certain ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey prepared by Calloway Land Surveyors LLC, J. Michael Ferreira, P.L.S., Connecticut License No. 12847, dated April 20, 2025, and last revised May 15, 2025, Drawing No. CLS-2025-0321." The Survey in the record is a different instrument: prepared by Thomas R. Pellegrino, P.L.S., License No. PLS-008741, Job No. CLS-2025-0417, plat dated April 28, 2025, and it describes a rectangle of 435.22 feet by 320.47 feet with bearings of S 78°15'30" E and S 11°44'30" W respectively.

*Analysis.* We computed the area enclosed by the Title Commitment's own courses using those bearings and distances: **approximately 279,535 square feet, or 6.42 acres** — almost exactly double the 139,392 square feet stated in the same document, in the Term Sheet, in the Resolution, in the Phase II ESA, and in the Survey. The two descriptions are not variants of the same parcel: they have different bearings (72°15'30" versus 78°15'30"), different dimensions, different surveyors, and different drawing numbers. They cannot both be right, and the Title Commitment is wrong on its face if the Survey is right. Three consequences follow. First, a lease that demises a parcel by a description that does not match the survey of record is a lease whose premises are undefined — the defect that most often produces a title exception that the lender will not accept. Second, the Survey and the title description cannot both support the ALTA certification required by Bayside's condition 6(d). Third, the recited area drives the $20.45 per square foot rent figure in Term Sheet Section 5; if the parcel were 279,535 square feet, the rent would be $10.19 per square foot, although the dollar rent itself would be unaffected. (As a related and much smaller point, the Survey's own courses compute to 139,475 square feet, 83 square feet more than the stated 139,392 — a 0.06% variance that is immaterial but that confirms the geometry should be confirmed by the surveyor before recording.)

*Position taken.* Section 2.2 provides that the Survey description governs, that the Title Commitment's Exhibit A is erroneous, that Exhibit A to the Lease consists exclusively of the Survey description, and that receipt of title policies reflecting the corrected description is a condition to the Lease Commencement Date. The stated area controls for all purposes. A joint boundary update is required before the first permit application. Exhibit A carries the surveyor's name, license number, and job number, and expressly disclaims the Ferreira drawing.

*Fallback.* If the title company will not amend Exhibit A before issuance, accept an insured-over description but require an ALTA 25-06 (same as survey) endorsement and a surveyor's affidavit, and shift the cost and risk of any later correction to Landlord.

*Open item.* Obtain the Ferreira drawing CLS-2025-0321 and have the surveyor of record confirm in writing which drawing and which description govern, and whether the 480-linear-foot bulkhead figure is a reference to a longer frontage than the surveyed eastern boundary. See Part VIII.

### Issue 2 — The Reverter Right Is the Deal, and It Must Be Repriced

The Term Sheet's New Lease right also does not state the priority of the new lease, does not require recognition of subleases, and does not run the cure periods from the new lease date — all of which Bayside requires.

*Position taken.* Article 10 is drafted to Bayside's checklist rather than to the Term Sheet: Section 10.1 (leasehold mortgage with no consent or fee), 10.2 (simultaneous notices, with an express consequence for failure), 10.3 (independent cure periods — 60/90/180 days, additional and not concurrent), 10.4 (New Lease on any termination, request within 60 days, execution within 30 days, effective as of termination, equal priority, subleases recognized, improvements included, no additional rent), 10.5 (no surrender or amendment without consent), 10.6 (foreclosure and assignment without consent), 10.7 (SNDA with the eight required elements), 10.8 (bankruptcy), and 10.9–10.11 (multiple mortgagees, no merger, mortgagee not obligated). "Leasehold Mortgagee" is defined broadly through "Qualified Mortgagee" so that the protections survive refinancing — the point you made about a lender in 2025 and a lender in 2065.

*Fallback.* None of these are tradeable in substance; if the Authority resists, the response is that these provisions are conditions to Bayside's closing and therefore to the deal.

### Issue 4 — The Tax Abatement Is Not Yet an Asset

**Severity: Critical. Sources: Term Sheet Section 10; Resolution (recital and Section 3(d)); Instructions Section 4; Title Commitment Exception No. 7; Bayside Term Sheet Section 6 (conditions).**

*Record facts.* The Term Sheet structures a fifteen-year phase-in at 25%, 50%, and 75% of full post-development assessed value, is explicit that the abatement "period shall commence on the Lease Commencement Date," and obligates the Authority only to "use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain all approvals and authorizations necessary to implement the tax abatement program." The Resolution recites that the abatement is "to be implemented through a separate tax abatement agreement between Meridian and the City of Port Calloway," and authorizes the Executive Director to execute such an agreement. No such agreement is in the record, and no City action appears anywhere in the record.

*Analysis.* (a) *Value.* At the projected $178,000,000 assessed value and 34.75 mills, full taxes would be $6,185,500 per year. Over fifteen years the un-abated burden would be $92,782,500; the abated burden is $46,391,250. The abatement is therefore worth **approximately $46.4 million in nominal dollars** — half the fifteen-year burden, and the single largest economic item in the deal after rent itself.

(b) *Timing.* Because the abatement clock starts on the Lease Commencement Date (October 1, 2025) but rent does not commence until October 1, 2028, roughly three of the fifteen Abatement Years are consumed before the Project produces income — and during those years the property is assessed as unimproved land at $4,200,000, so the abatement delivers almost nothing ($36,488 per year at the 25% tier) while the 2038–2040 years, which would otherwise fall at the 75% tier, fall at 100%. Deferring the start to the Rent Commencement Date is worth approximately **$4.6 million** in nominal terms on unchanged assumptions (three years at $1,546,375 of forgone abatement). This is precisely the point in your instructions about maximizing the benefit during the income-producing years.

(c) *Enforceability.* The Authority is a redevelopment authority; it does not levy or collect real property taxes. The City's assessor, Board of Finance, and legislative body do. A promise by the Authority to provide an abatement is therefore not self-executing, and "commercially reasonable efforts" is not an enforceable commitment to deliver value. The statutory vehicle by which a Connecticut municipality may fix assessments or abate taxes for a commercial project must be confirmed with municipal counsel, together with the permissible duration; the record identifies none, and a fifteen-year phase-in may exceed what the enabling authority permits. This is a diligence question we cannot answer from the record and should be put to Howard Koss in writing early.

(d) *Interaction with the tax covenant.* Under a triple-net structure you covenant to pay all taxes. If the abatement fails, the covenant produces the opposite of the underwritten economics, and the Term Sheet gives you no remedy.

*Position taken.* Section 6.3(b) requires a recorded, City-executed, Tenant-enforceable tax abatement agreement as a condition to the Lease Commencement Date; Section 6.3(a) fixes the Abatement Commencement Date at the later of the Rent Commencement Date and the first year in which the Project is assessed as improved property; Section 6.3(c) upgrades "commercially reasonable efforts" to diligent efforts with a representation that no undisclosed municipal action is required; and Section 6.4 provides a dollar-for-dollar Base Rent offset for any shortfall, plus a termination right if the shortfall persists for two consecutive Abatement Years or exceeds $3,000,000. Section 6.2 excludes PILOT payments and taxes on the adjoining parcel.

*Fallback.* If the Authority insists that the abatement begin on the Lease Commencement Date, quantify the concession at approximately $4.6 million and trade it for a corresponding reduction elsewhere — most efficiently, an equivalent rent abatement in the first two Rent Years, which produces nearly the same after-tax effect and requires no City action. If the City will not commit in a recorded agreement before closing, require an escrow or a Base Rent offset (Section 6.4) as the commercial substitute, and do not sign without one of the two.

*Open item.* Confirm (i) the statutory authority for and permissible duration of the abatement; (ii) whether any special taxing district levy applies in addition to the 34.75 mill City rate; and (iii) that the City will be the contracting party. See Part VIII.
MDEOF

### Issue 5 — Percentage Rent: A Participation Mechanism That Becomes a Gross Receipts Tax

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 6; Instructions Section 3.**

*Record facts.* Percentage rent is 2.0% of annual Gross Revenues above a $28,500,000 Breakpoint, commencing in "Lease Year 6." Term Sheet Section 6 states that the Breakpoint "is a fixed dollar amount and shall remain unchanged for the duration of the Lease Term," and that specific exclusions from Gross Revenues "shall be defined in the Definitive Lease." Gross Revenues are defined as all rents, fees, charges, and other income of every kind generated from the operation of the Project. Percentage rent statements are to be prepared "in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles consistently applied," with books and records kept for three years and an annual Landlord audit right with a 5% cost-shifting threshold.

*Analysis.* The Term Sheet's structure produces a mismatch that grows without limit. Base Rent escalates at a fixed 2.5%; the Breakpoint does not escalate at all. Percentage rent is therefore levied on an ever-larger real base, and the effective participation rate rises every year in real terms. On an illustrative path of $30,000,000 of Gross Revenues in Rent Year 6 growing at 3% per annum (the record contains no revenue pro forma, so this is ours, not the parties'), percentage rent rises from $30,000 in Year 6 to $8.8 million in Year 99, and from about 0.9% of Base Rent to about 30% of Base Rent. Aggregated over Rent Years 6 through 99, the difference between a fixed Breakpoint and an indexed Breakpoint is approximately **$146 million** ($248.3 million versus $102.4 million). That is the difference between a participation in upside and a second ground rent. The Term Sheet's own words support your reading: it is an additional rent "in the form of Percentage Rent... in excess of" a Breakpoint, that is, a share of performance above an assumed level — not a levy that increases merely because of inflation.

Three secondary defects: (a) "Lease Year 6" is ambiguous in the Term Sheet, which uses "Lease Year" to mean both a Term Year (Section 3) and a period beginning on the Rent Commencement Date (Section 5); the difference is three years of percentage rent. (b) Measuring Gross Revenues on a GAAP accrual basis imports straight-line rent recognition and non-cash adjustments, which can exceed cash actually received. (c) The audit right is not time-limited, so a statement delivered in Year 10 could in principle be audited in Year 30.

*Position taken.* Section 4.2 indexes the Breakpoint in lockstep with Base Rent so that the Year 6 relationship (8.84 times Base Rent) is preserved for the Term, with the stated intent in Section 4.2(d) that the provision be construed as a participation in upside and not a gross receipts tax. Section 4.3 measures Gross Revenues on a cash receipts basis. Section 4.4 contains a closed list of seventeen exclusions implementing your instructions — deposits, utility reimbursements, operating expense recoveries, insurance proceeds, condemnation awards, financing proceeds, investment income, capital cost reimbursements, remediation recoveries, government payments, affiliate rent above arm's length, public open space revenue, late fees, and pre-commencement receipts. Sections 4.6(b) and 4.7 impose a 24-month audit lookback and a deemed-acceptance rule. Section 1.1 defines "Term Year" and "Rent Year" separately, with a drafting note explaining why.

*Fallback.* If the Authority refuses full lockstep indexing, a partial index is still far better than none: index the Breakpoint annually at the lesser of 2.5% and CPI, or reset it at each ten-year CPI Reset Date. Note that the Term Sheet expressly delegates the exclusions to the definitive lease, so the Section 4.4 list should not be treated as a deviation at all — press that point.

*Client note.* This is a knowing departure from an express Term Sheet term ("shall remain unchanged"). Expect Board review under Resolution Section 4(d).

### Issue 6 — The ELUR Prohibits Ground-Floor Residential Use and the Project Program Assumes It

**Severity: High. Sources: Phase II ESA Sections 2.3 and 7; Term Sheet Section 4 (Project Overview and Environmental Restrictions); Title Commitment Exception No. 1; Survey Section 3(c).**

*Record facts.* The ELUR prohibits "residential use" on the ground floor, defined as "habitable space at or below finished grade elevation intended for residential dwelling, sleeping, cooking, or eating purposes." The Term Sheet's Project description includes "ground-floor residential lobby and amenity spaces (fitness center, package room, resident lounge, and leasing office)." The Phase II ESA states that the ELUR "does not... expressly define whether ancillary residential spaces... constitute 'residential use,'" calls this "a significant interpretive ambiguity that could expose the Client to potential enforcement action by CT DEEP," and recommends (i) obtaining a formal DEEP interpretation or variance before finalizing design and the lease, (ii) limiting ground-floor uses to commercial, retail, and clearly non-habitable functions in the absence of clarification, and (iii) locating affordable units exclusively on upper floors.

*Analysis.* The Lease cannot cure the ambiguity, but it can allocate it. As drafted in the Term Sheet, nothing obliges the Authority — the party that created the ELUR, negotiated it with DEEP, and holds the fee — to help resolve the question, and nothing protects you if DEEP takes a restrictive view after you have spent $50 million on foundations. The affordable housing requirement interacts awkwardly as well: the recorded covenant requires 15% affordable units but says nothing about floor location, while the ELUR restricts the ground floor.

*Position taken.* Section 9.3 defines the permitted ground-floor program (retail and commercial tenancies plus non-habitable ancillary functions), requires Affordable Units on the second floor and above, and provides that a DEEP determination will not constitute a Tenant default. Section 5.6 obliges Landlord to join applications and consents as record owner, to cooperate in obtaining a DEEP interpretation or ELUR modification, and — if an adverse determination becomes final and no modification is obtained within twelve months — gives Tenant an election to redesign or to terminate with return of the Security Deposit, cash-out of the unapplied Remediation Credit, and no reverter or liquidated damages. Section 2.6(a)(viii) makes the DEEP confirmation a condition to the Lease Commencement Date.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not accept the pre-closing DEEP confirmation as a condition, preserve the post-closing termination right in Section 5.6(d) — the economic protection matters more than the timing. If DEEP declines to opine, obtain a written opinion of environmental counsel that lobby and amenity space are not "habitable space" and rely on Section 5.6(b), which bars Landlord from asserting an ELUR violation absent a written DEEP determination.

### Issue 7 — The Mechanics' Lien Is Being Passed to You as a Permitted Exception

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 13(6); Title Commitment Schedule B-I Requirement No. 7 and Schedule B-II Exception No. 6; Survey Section 3(d)(iii).**

*Record facts.* Calloway Marine Demolition Inc. filed a mechanics' lien on April 3, 2025 in the amount of $187,500 (Volume 418, Page 302) for bulkhead demolition on the Premises, "against the fee simple interest of the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority as record owner," for work "performed on the land prior to the execution of any lease." The Title Commitment states that "[t]he Company will not issue either policy described in Schedule A until this requirement has been satisfied," and that until then the lien "shall remain as an exception to coverage." The Survey observes evidence of partial bulkhead demolition consistent with the lien, including removal of approximately 40 linear feet of concrete cap.

*Analysis.* The Term Sheet lists the lien as a Permitted Exception to be "carried into the Definitive Lease" — which would leave you holding a title defect arising entirely from the Authority's own pre-lease work on its own fee. That is inconsistent with the Title Commitment's Requirement No. 7 and with Bayside's condition that the loan policy be subject to no exceptions other than those it has approved. It is also a warning about the bulkhead: demolition work was performed and the lien is unpaid, which suggests a contractor dispute that may not be confined to money.

*Position taken.* Section 17.1(g) makes discharge, bonding under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37, or an acceptable insured-over the Authority's obligation at its sole cost, on or before the Lease Commencement Date; Exhibit I expressly states that the lien is **not** a Permitted Exception; and Section 6.7 relieves Tenant of any special assessment attributable to the pre-lease demolition work.

*Fallback.* If the Authority bonds off the lien rather than discharging it, require (i) a surety acceptable to the title company and to Bayside, (ii) an indemnity from the Authority, and (iii) confirmation that Tenant is not named in any action and that the bonded claim cannot attach to the leasehold.

### Issue 8 — The Recorded Right of First Refusal Does Not Contemplate the Financing

**Severity: Critical (as a closing condition). Sources: Title Commitment Exception No. 4; Term Sheet Section 11; Bayside Term Sheet Sections 5.1 and 5.6.**

*Record facts.* The right of first refusal is not created by the Term Sheet; it is already of record, in a "Declaration of Right of First Refusal dated September 8, 2019, and recorded at Volume 405, Page 55," granting the Authority the right to "repurchase or reacquire the leasehold interest in the land in the event the Tenant proposes an assignment of the leasehold estate to a non-affiliated entity at any time during the first twenty (20) years of the lease term." The Title Commitment says expressly: "The Right of First Refusal, as recorded, does not by its terms contain any exception or carve-out for transfers resulting from foreclosure, deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, the exercise of remedies by a leasehold mortgagee, or assignments by a leasehold mortgagee or its designee following a foreclosure or acceptance of a deed-in-lieu."

*Analysis.* Two problems. First, breadth: a right of first refusal on any "assignment of the leasehold estate" or of "any interest therein" can be read to capture the grant of the leasehold mortgage itself, which Bayside's Section 5.1 says must require no consent, approval, joinder, or fee from the Landlord. Second, priority: even on a narrow reading, a foreclosure sale transfer or a deed in lieu would arguably trigger the ROFR, which collides with Bayside Section 5.6 (no Landlord consent or approval required for foreclosure and assignment) and would chill a foreclosure bidder. Because the instrument is recorded and binds successors, a lease provision alone cannot fix it: the recorded declaration must be amended, and the amendment recorded, before the title company will issue the loan policy without an exception.

A related diligence point: a right of first refusal recorded in 2019, and an affordable housing covenant recorded in 2019, both in favor of the Authority and both referencing a "leasehold estate," suggest an earlier transaction with a prior developer. The record does not include either instrument or any prior lease, option, or disposition agreement.

*Position taken.* Section 11.5 limits the ROFR to the twenty-year period, applies it only to a Transfer of the Lease in whole for value, and adds a closing deadline and lapse mechanism. Section 11.6(a) contains eight carve-outs (leasehold mortgages; foreclosure and deed-in-lieu transfers; Permitted Transfers; subleases; equity transfers; involuntary transfers; replacement-developer transfers; condemnation conveyances). Section 11.6(b)–(c) recites the recorded declaration, identifies both defects, and requires an amendment, executed and recorded at Landlord's cost, as a condition to the Lease Commencement Date; Section 2.6(a)(ix) makes that a condition precedent.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not amend the recorded declaration, obtain (i) a recorded subordination of the ROFR Declaration to the Leasehold Mortgages, and (ii) a no-merger and non-disturbance acknowledgment in the SNDA. Do not accept an unrecorded side letter.

### Issue 9 — Remediation: Uncapped Overruns, an Understated Estimate, and a Credit That Arrives Late

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 7; Phase II ESA Sections 6 and 7; Instructions Section 5; Bayside Term Sheet Section 6(e).**

*Record facts.* The remediation estimate is $2,400,000 ($1,850,000 for the 4,200 SF Northwest Corner area and $550,000 for the 1,600 SF Former Dry Dock area). The Authority provides a $1,800,000 credit against the first monthly rent payments, and Tenant bears $600,000 plus "any actual remediation costs in excess of the $2,400,000 estimate." The credit is applied in Base Rent Months 1 through 7 at $0 rent, plus $137,500 in Month 8.

*Analysis.* The credit arithmetic reconciles ($237,500 × 7 = $1,662,500; plus $137,500 = $1,800,000; Month 8 rent of $100,000). The exposure does not. Three findings from our recomputation of the ESA:

> (i) **The contingency is mislabeled.** The Area 1 table shows $1,750,000 of pre-contingency line items and a "Contingency (10%)" of $100,000 — which is 5.71%, not 10%. Area 2 shows $525,000 of line items and $25,000 of contingency — 4.76%. Applying the stated 10% yields $1,925,000 and $577,500, for a corrected total of **$2,502,500**, or $102,500 more than the estimate. (Exhibit H to the Draft Lease states this.)
>
> (ii) **The estimate excludes the work that makes remediation lawful.** The RAP, the Soil Management Plan, DEEP fees, the post-remediation verification report, any ELUR modification, and legal and consulting fees are all excluded, as is groundwater dewatering and treatment (expressly), and the bulkhead (expressly). These are not optional: Section 7 of the Term Sheet requires a DEEP-approved RAP, an LEP, and verification.
>
> (iii) **The volume assumption is aggressive.** The ESA computes 933 cubic yards of in-situ impact (4,200 SF × 6 ft ÷ 27) but assumes 3,100 cubic yards of material handling — a 3.3x over-excavation factor. That is defensible if the delineation is conservative, but it is an assumption, not a measured quantity, and it should be tested in bid.

Two further points. First, timing: you fund the remediation in cash during construction (2026–2028) and receive the credit only after October 1, 2028, spread over eight months. On $2.4 million, that is roughly two years of carry — a real cost the Term Sheet does not recognize. Second, sequencing risk: if this Lease terminates before the credit is exhausted (casualty, permit failure, ELUR determination, reverter), the Term Sheet gives you nothing back.

*Position taken.* Section 5.3 fixes the credit mechanics with a table, makes the credit unconditional and non-setoff-able, permits acceleration at Tenant's election, allows application against taxes and insurance if rent commencement is delayed beyond 40 months, and requires cash payment of any unapplied balance on termination. Section 5.4 creates cost bands: Tenant to $2,400,000; Tenant to $3,000,000; above $3,000,000, Landlord bears costs attributable to undisclosed, off-site, groundwater, or non-footprint conditions, and shares the balance 50/50; and above a $4,500,000 revised estimate, Tenant may terminate with return of the deposit. Section 5.1 adds Landlord environmental representations, and Section 5.8 adds a Landlord indemnity for pre-existing and off-site conditions — which the Term Sheet omits entirely and which is the largest single gap in the environmental allocation.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not accept an uncapped Landlord responsibility for undisclosed conditions, accept a fixed Landlord contribution (e.g., an additional $1,000,000 credit if remediation exceeds $3,000,000) and retain the walk-away right at a higher threshold. If the Authority will not move at all, require a pollution legal liability policy with a remediation cost-cap feature as a closing condition and price the retained risk in your own contingency.

### Issue 10 — The Bulkhead: Unpriced, Unallocated, and Described Inconsistently

**Severity: High. Sources: Phase II ESA Sections 5 and 7 (Recommendation 8); Survey Sections 1 and 3(b); Term Sheet (silent); Title Commitment Exception No. 6; Instructions (silent).**

*Record facts.* The ESA describes the bulkhead as "reinforced concrete and timber construction," in "fair to poor" condition, with "lateral displacement, longitudinal and transverse cracking, deteriorated and missing timber lagging, and evidence of erosion of backfill," recommends an independent structural engineering assessment, and states that "bulkhead repair or replacement costs are not included in the environmental remediation cost estimates." The Survey describes the same structure as "steel sheet piling with a concrete cap," with spalling and corrosion, and notes removal of approximately 40 linear feet of cap. The bulkhead sits at or near the eastern edge of the 15-foot public pedestrian access easement, which "prohibits the construction of permanent structures within the easement area."

*Analysis.* Neither the Term Sheet nor the Instructions address the bulkhead, and the $425,000,000 sources and uses do not identify a bulkhead line item. For a waterfront site in Flood Zone AE where 60% of the grade is below the base flood elevation, the bulkhead is a structural and insurance issue as much as an environmental one, and its replacement cost on 480 linear feet (or 320 feet, per the Survey geometry) is material. Two conflicts must be resolved before anyone can bid the work: which description of the structure is correct, and how much of it is even within the Premises given the easement prohibition on permanent structures. Add to that the possibility that the City, as holder of the pedestrian easement and as the party whose contractor did the demolition, will assert an interest in the design and condition of the structure.

*Position taken.* Section 9.6(b) allocates the pre-existing-deterioration component to Landlord, determined by a jointly engaged marine structural engineer (or by the Expert procedure), with Landlord's share payable or creditable against Base Rent; the Project-driven component remains a Tenant hard cost. Section 2.3 confirms Tenant's right to reconstruct the bulkhead and Section 9.6(c) allocates post-commencement maintenance to Tenant. Section 6.7 excludes special assessments relating to the pre-lease demolition.

*Fallback.* A fixed dollar credit (to be priced once the engineering assessment is complete) is often easier for a public landlord to approve than an open-ended obligation. Commission the structural assessment now — it is a condition to any allocation.

### Issue 11 — The Milestone Schedule Has No Cushion Against the Loan, the Guaranty, or Entitlement

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Sections 3 and 9; Bayside Term Sheet Sections 2, 4, and 6(k); Phase II ESA Section 5.**

*Record facts.* Milestones fall at 18, 42, 60, and 84 months from the Lease Commencement Date (April 1, 2027; April 1, 2029; October 1, 2030; October 1, 2032 on a October 1, 2025 commencement). Force majeure extensions are capped at 12 months in the aggregate, plus 6 months for permitting, for 18 months total. The Bayside loan is for 48 months with two 6-month extensions (60 months maximum). Coventry's completion guaranty to Bayside guarantees "lien-free completion of the Project... on or before the Initial Maturity Date."

*Analysis.* Read together, four schedule problems appear:

> (i) **Zero cushion at Milestone 3.** The final extended loan maturity (60 months) and the Milestone 3 deadline (60 months) are the same day. A project that is one month late is simultaneously in milestone default and past loan maturity.
>
> (ii) **The completion guaranty is 12–30 months tighter than the lease.** Coventry guarantees completion by month 48; the lease permits Phase 1 as late as month 60, and with the 18-month force majeure and permitting allowance, as late as month 78 (April 1, 2032).
>
> (iii) **Phase 2 is outside the loan term.** Milestone 4 (October 1, 2032) is 24 months after the last possible loan maturity; the office building therefore depends on a refinancing or on separate capitalization that is not in the record.
>
> (iv) **Entitlement risk is compressed into Milestone 1.** Construction must commence within 18 months, which requires site plan approval, zoning approvals, coastal and wetlands approvals, building permits, and DEEP approvals for the RAP and Soil Management Plan — with the ELUR ambiguity unresolved and a litigable affordable housing covenant. The ESA also documents a November 2024 nor'easter that put water at approximately 10.5 feet NAVD88 at the bulkhead, and recommends calibrating force majeure provisions to coastal storm risk. The Term Sheet's force majeure list ("acts of God, war, terrorism, civil unrest, strikes, labor disputes, governmental orders or moratoria, pandemics, epidemics, and similar events") does not mention named storms, tidal flooding, storm surge, supply chain disruption (which you specifically raised), or Landlord-caused delay.

*Position taken.* Section 7.4 expands the force majeure list (named storms, tidal flooding and storm surge, FEMA map changes, shortages and supply chain disruption, utility delays, unknown site conditions) and requires only that notice affect the extension by the days of delay in giving it. Section 7.2(c) adds day-for-day extensions for delays attributable to the ELUR, Landlord's title, or the City, outside the 18-month caps. Section 7.2(d) adds a no-penalty termination right if Phase 1 approvals are finally denied. Section 7.5 removes any consequence for a milestone achieved within the cure period. Section 18.9 makes time of the essence for rent and for the closing conditions, but not for the Milestones.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not expand force majeure, seek a single additional 6-month extension available on written notice without a showing of cause. Separately, and as a matter of internal project management, consider re-basing the loan extension conditions and the Coventry guaranty trigger so that the guarantor's obligation is tied to the lease milestones rather than the initial maturity.

### Issue 12 — Security Deposit: The Step-Down Is Undefined and the Draw Standard Is Loose

**Severity: Medium-High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 8; Instructions Section 5; Bayside Term Sheet Section 4; Resolution (recital).**

*Record facts.* The deposit is $5,700,000 (24 months of initial Base Rent), reducible to $2,850,000 (12 months) "upon Tenant's demonstration to Landlord's reasonable satisfaction that the Project has achieved and maintained an overall occupancy rate of ninety percent (90%) or greater for a period of twenty-four (24) consecutive months." Landlord may draw "upon the occurrence of any uncured Event of Default." The Resolution recital describes a letter of credit "issued by a federally chartered banking institution"; the Term Sheet requires a bank "organized under the laws of the United States or any state thereof" with an A-/A3 rating; Bayside permits a cash deposit at Borrower's option.

*Analysis.* "Overall occupancy rate" is undefined for a mixed-use project with residential, office, and retail components; there is no specification of physical versus economic occupancy, no measurement date, no certification standard, no objection period, no deemed-approval mechanism, and no timetable for the reduction after the condition is met — four separate sources of dispute, exactly as you anticipated. The draw standard ("any uncured Event of Default") would allow a draw for a non-monetary default and for claimed damages, without an accounting. The three form-of-instrument formulations conflict.

*Position taken.* Section 8.3 defines "Occupancy Rate" as leased-and-occupied rentable square footage over delivered and available rentable square footage, requires a chief financial officer's certificate with a rent roll, imposes a 10-Business-Day objection period with deemed approval, references the Expert for disputes, and makes the reduction a one-time, non-revocable reduction with a 10-Business-Day implementation deadline. Section 8.4 limits draws to monetary obligations then due or documented direct damages, requires 10 Business Days' notice to Tenant and each Leasehold Mortgagee, bars draws on good-faith-disputed amounts and on amounts the mortgagee has cured, and requires an accounting and repayment of improper draws with interest. Section 8.2 expressly permits state-chartered banks and a cash alternative. Section 8.5 defers replenishment of disputed amounts.

*Fallback.* If the Authority insists on "reasonable satisfaction," at least fix the objective inputs (rent roll plus certification) and a 15-Business-Day deemed-approval period; without a deemed-approval mechanic the step-down will not be operationally achievable.
MDEOF
