*Position taken.* Section 4.2 indexes the Breakpoint in lockstep with Base Rent so that the Year 6 relationship (8.84 times Base Rent) is preserved for the Term, with the stated intent in Section 4.2(d) that the provision be construed as a participation in upside and not a gross receipts tax. Section 4.3 measures Gross Revenues on a cash receipts basis. Section 4.4 contains a closed list of seventeen exclusions implementing your instructions — deposits, utility reimbursements, operating expense recoveries, insurance proceeds, condemnation awards, financing proceeds, investment income, capital cost reimbursements, remediation recoveries, government payments, affiliate rent above arm's length, public open space revenue, late fees, and pre-commencement receipts. Sections 4.6(b) and 4.7 impose a 24-month audit lookback and a deemed-acceptance rule. Section 1.1 defines "Term Year" and "Rent Year" separately, with a drafting note explaining why.

*Fallback.* If the Authority refuses full lockstep indexing, a partial index is still far better than none: index the Breakpoint annually at the lesser of 2.5% and CPI, or reset it at each ten-year CPI Reset Date. Note that the Term Sheet expressly delegates the exclusions to the definitive lease, so the Section 4.4 list should not be treated as a deviation at all — press that point.

*Client note.* This is a knowing departure from an express Term Sheet term ("shall remain unchanged"). Expect Board review under Resolution Section 4(d).

### Issue 6 — The ELUR Prohibits Ground-Floor Residential Use and the Project Program Assumes It

**Severity: High. Sources: Phase II ESA Sections 2.3 and 7; Term Sheet Section 4 (Project Overview and Environmental Restrictions); Title Commitment Exception No. 1; Survey Section 3(c).**

*Record facts.* The ELUR prohibits "residential use" on the ground floor, defined as "habitable space at or below finished grade elevation intended for residential dwelling, sleeping, cooking, or eating purposes." The Term Sheet's Project description includes "ground-floor residential lobby and amenity spaces (fitness center, package room, resident lounge, and leasing office)." The Phase II ESA states that the ELUR "does not... expressly define whether ancillary residential spaces... constitute 'residential use,'" calls this "a significant interpretive ambiguity that could expose the Client to potential enforcement action by CT DEEP," and recommends (i) obtaining a formal DEEP interpretation or variance before finalizing design and the lease, (ii) limiting ground-floor uses to commercial, retail, and clearly non-habitable functions in the absence of clarification, and (iii) locating affordable units exclusively on upper floors.

*Analysis.* The Lease cannot cure the ambiguity, but it can allocate it. As drafted in the Term Sheet, nothing obliges the Authority — the party that created the ELUR, negotiated it with DEEP, and holds the fee — to help resolve the question, and nothing protects you if DEEP takes a restrictive view after you have spent $50 million on foundations. The affordable housing requirement interacts awkwardly as well: the recorded covenant requires 15% affordable units but says nothing about floor location, while the ELUR restricts the ground floor.

*Position taken.* Section 9.3 defines the permitted ground-floor program (retail and commercial tenancies plus non-habitable ancillary functions), requires Affordable Units on the second floor and above, and provides that a DEEP determination will not constitute a Tenant default. Section 5.6 obliges Landlord to join applications and consents as record owner, to cooperate in obtaining a DEEP interpretation or ELUR modification, and — if an adverse determination becomes final and no modification is obtained within twelve months — gives Tenant an election to redesign or to terminate with return of the Security Deposit, cash-out of the unapplied Remediation Credit, and no reverter or liquidated damages. Section 2.6(a)(viii) makes the DEEP confirmation a condition to the Lease Commencement Date.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not accept the pre-closing DEEP confirmation as a condition, preserve the post-closing termination right in Section 5.6(d) — the economic protection matters more than the timing. If DEEP declines to opine, obtain a written opinion of environmental counsel that lobby and amenity space are not "habitable space" and rely on Section 5.6(b), which bars Landlord from asserting an ELUR violation absent a written DEEP determination.

### Issue 7 — The Mechanics' Lien Is Being Passed to You as a Permitted Exception

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 13(6); Title Commitment Schedule B-I Requirement No. 7 and Schedule B-II Exception No. 6; Survey Section 3(d)(iii).**

*Record facts.* Calloway Marine Demolition Inc. filed a mechanics' lien on April 3, 2025 in the amount of $187,500 (Volume 418, Page 302) for bulkhead demolition on the Premises, "against the fee simple interest of the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority as record owner," for work "performed on the land prior to the execution of any lease." The Title Commitment states that "[t]he Company will not issue either policy described in Schedule A until this requirement has been satisfied," and that until then the lien "shall remain as an exception to coverage." The Survey observes evidence of partial bulkhead demolition consistent with the lien, including removal of approximately 40 linear feet of concrete cap.

*Analysis.* The Term Sheet lists the lien as a Permitted Exception to be "carried into the Definitive Lease" — which would leave you holding a title defect arising entirely from the Authority's own pre-lease work on its own fee. That is inconsistent with the Title Commitment's Requirement No. 7 and with Bayside's condition that the loan policy be subject to no exceptions other than those it has approved. It is also a warning about the bulkhead: demolition work was performed and the lien is unpaid, which suggests a contractor dispute that may not be confined to money.

*Position taken.* Section 17.1(g) makes discharge, bonding under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37, or an acceptable insured-over the Authority's obligation at its sole cost, on or before the Lease Commencement Date; Exhibit I expressly states that the lien is **not** a Permitted Exception; and Section 6.7 relieves Tenant of any special assessment attributable to the pre-lease demolition work.

*Fallback.* If the Authority bonds off the lien rather than discharging it, require (i) a surety acceptable to the title company and to Bayside, (ii) an indemnity from the Authority, and (iii) confirmation that Tenant is not named in any action and that the bonded claim cannot attach to the leasehold.

### Issue 8 — The Recorded Right of First Refusal Does Not Contemplate the Financing

**Severity: Critical (as a closing condition). Sources: Title Commitment Exception No. 4; Term Sheet Section 11; Bayside Term Sheet Sections 5.1 and 5.6.**

*Record facts.* The right of first refusal is not created by the Term Sheet; it is already of record, in a "Declaration of Right of First Refusal dated September 8, 2019, and recorded at Volume 405, Page 55," granting the Authority the right to "repurchase or reacquire the leasehold interest in the land in the event the Tenant proposes an assignment of the leasehold estate to a non-affiliated entity at any time during the first twenty (20) years of the lease term." The Title Commitment says expressly: "The Right of First Refusal, as recorded, does not by its terms contain any exception or carve-out for transfers resulting from foreclosure, deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, the exercise of remedies by a leasehold mortgagee, or assignments by a leasehold mortgagee or its designee following a foreclosure or acceptance of a deed-in-lieu."

*Analysis.* Two problems. First, breadth: a right of first refusal on any "assignment of the leasehold estate" or of "any interest therein" can be read to capture the grant of the leasehold mortgage itself, which Bayside's Section 5.1 says must require no consent, approval, joinder, or fee from the Landlord. Second, priority: even on a narrow reading, a foreclosure sale transfer or a deed in lieu would arguably trigger the ROFR, which collides with Bayside Section 5.6 (no Landlord consent or approval required for foreclosure and assignment) and would chill a foreclosure bidder. Because the instrument is recorded and binds successors, a lease provision alone cannot fix it: the recorded declaration must be amended, and the amendment recorded, before the title company will issue the loan policy without an exception.

A related diligence point: a right of first refusal recorded in 2019, and an affordable housing covenant recorded in 2019, both in favor of the Authority and both referencing a "leasehold estate," suggest an earlier transaction with a prior developer. The record does not include either instrument or any prior lease, option, or disposition agreement.

*Position taken.* Section 11.5 limits the ROFR to the twenty-year period, applies it only to a Transfer of the Lease in whole for value, and adds a closing deadline and lapse mechanism. Section 11.6(a) contains eight carve-outs (leasehold mortgages; foreclosure and deed-in-lieu transfers; Permitted Transfers; subleases; equity transfers; involuntary transfers; replacement-developer transfers; condemnation conveyances). Section 11.6(b)–(c) recites the recorded declaration, identifies both defects, and requires an amendment, executed and recorded at Landlord's cost, as a condition to the Lease Commencement Date; Section 2.6(a)(ix) makes that a condition precedent.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not amend the recorded declaration, obtain (i) a recorded subordination of the ROFR Declaration to the Leasehold Mortgages, and (ii) a no-merger and non-disturbance acknowledgment in the SNDA. Do not accept an unrecorded side letter.

### Issue 9 — Remediation: Uncapped Overruns, an Understated Estimate, and a Credit That Arrives Late

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 7; Phase II ESA Sections 6 and 7; Instructions Section 5; Bayside Term Sheet Section 6(e).**

*Record facts.* The remediation estimate is $2,400,000 ($1,850,000 for the 4,200 SF Northwest Corner area and $550,000 for the 1,600 SF Former Dry Dock area). The Authority provides a $1,800,000 credit against the first monthly rent payments, and Tenant bears $600,000 plus "any actual remediation costs in excess of the $2,400,000 estimate." The credit is applied in Base Rent Months 1 through 7 at $0 rent, plus $137,500 in Month 8.

*Analysis.* The credit arithmetic reconciles ($237,500 × 7 = $1,662,500; plus $137,500 = $1,800,000; Month 8 rent of $100,000). The exposure does not. Three findings from our recomputation of the ESA:

> (i) **The contingency is mislabeled.** The Area 1 table shows $1,750,000 of pre-contingency line items and a "Contingency (10%)" of $100,000 — which is 5.71%, not 10%. Area 2 shows $525,000 of line items and $25,000 of contingency — 4.76%. Applying the stated 10% yields $1,925,000 and $577,500, for a corrected total of **$2,502,500**, or $102,500 more than the estimate. (Exhibit H to the Draft Lease states this.)
>
> (ii) **The estimate excludes the work that makes remediation lawful.** The RAP, the Soil Management Plan, DEEP fees, the post-remediation verification report, any ELUR modification, and legal and consulting fees are all excluded, as is groundwater dewatering and treatment (expressly), and the bulkhead (expressly). These are not optional: Section 7 of the Term Sheet requires a DEEP-approved RAP, an LEP, and verification.
>
> (iii) **The volume assumption is aggressive.** The ESA computes 933 cubic yards of in-situ impact (4,200 SF × 6 ft ÷ 27) but assumes 3,100 cubic yards of material handling — a 3.3x over-excavation factor. That is defensible if the delineation is conservative, but it is an assumption, not a measured quantity, and it should be tested in bid.

Two further points. First, timing: you fund the remediation in cash during construction (2026–2028) and receive the credit only after October 1, 2028, spread over eight months. On $2.4 million, that is roughly two years of carry — a real cost the Term Sheet does not recognize. Second, sequencing risk: if this Lease terminates before the credit is exhausted (casualty, permit failure, ELUR determination, reverter), the Term Sheet gives you nothing back.

*Position taken.* Section 5.3 fixes the credit mechanics with a table, makes the credit unconditional and non-setoff-able, permits acceleration at Tenant's election, allows application against taxes and insurance if rent commencement is delayed beyond 40 months, and requires cash payment of any unapplied balance on termination. Section 5.4 creates cost bands: Tenant to $2,400,000; Tenant to $3,000,000; above $3,000,000, Landlord bears costs attributable to undisclosed, off-site, groundwater, or non-footprint conditions, and shares the balance 50/50; and above a $4,500,000 revised estimate, Tenant may terminate with return of the deposit. Section 5.1 adds Landlord environmental representations, and Section 5.8 adds a Landlord indemnity for pre-existing and off-site conditions — which the Term Sheet omits entirely and which is the largest single gap in the environmental allocation.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not accept an uncapped Landlord responsibility for undisclosed conditions, accept a fixed Landlord contribution (e.g., an additional $1,000,000 credit if remediation exceeds $3,000,000) and retain the walk-away right at a higher threshold. If the Authority will not move at all, require a pollution legal liability policy with a remediation cost-cap feature as a closing condition and price the retained risk in your own contingency.

### Issue 10 — The Bulkhead: Unpriced, Unallocated, and Described Inconsistently

**Severity: High. Sources: Phase II ESA Sections 5 and 7 (Recommendation 8); Survey Sections 1 and 3(b); Term Sheet (silent); Title Commitment Exception No. 6; Instructions (silent).**

*Record facts.* The ESA describes the bulkhead as "reinforced concrete and timber construction," in "fair to poor" condition, with "lateral displacement, longitudinal and transverse cracking, deteriorated and missing timber lagging, and evidence of erosion of backfill," recommends an independent structural engineering assessment, and states that "bulkhead repair or replacement costs are not included in the environmental remediation cost estimates." The Survey describes the same structure as "steel sheet piling with a concrete cap," with spalling and corrosion, and notes removal of approximately 40 linear feet of cap. The bulkhead sits at or near the eastern edge of the 15-foot public pedestrian access easement, which "prohibits the construction of permanent structures within the easement area."

*Analysis.* Neither the Term Sheet nor the Instructions address the bulkhead, and the $425,000,000 sources and uses do not identify a bulkhead line item. For a waterfront site in Flood Zone AE where 60% of the grade is below the base flood elevation, the bulkhead is a structural and insurance issue as much as an environmental one, and its replacement cost on 480 linear feet (or 320 feet, per the Survey geometry) is material. Two conflicts must be resolved before anyone can bid the work: which description of the structure is correct, and how much of it is even within the Premises given the easement prohibition on permanent structures. Add to that the possibility that the City, as holder of the pedestrian easement and as the party whose contractor did the demolition, will assert an interest in the design and condition of the structure.

*Position taken.* Section 9.6(b) allocates the pre-existing-deterioration component to Landlord, determined by a jointly engaged marine structural engineer (or by the Expert procedure), with Landlord's share payable or creditable against Base Rent; the Project-driven component remains a Tenant hard cost. Section 2.3 confirms Tenant's right to reconstruct the bulkhead and Section 9.6(c) allocates post-commencement maintenance to Tenant. Section 6.7 excludes special assessments relating to the pre-lease demolition.

*Fallback.* A fixed dollar credit (to be priced once the engineering assessment is complete) is often easier for a public landlord to approve than an open-ended obligation. Commission the structural assessment now — it is a condition to any allocation.

### Issue 11 — The Milestone Schedule Has No Cushion Against the Loan, the Guaranty, or Entitlement

**Severity: High. Sources: Term Sheet Sections 3 and 9; Bayside Term Sheet Sections 2, 4, and 6(k); Phase II ESA Section 5.**

*Record facts.* Milestones fall at 18, 42, 60, and 84 months from the Lease Commencement Date (April 1, 2027; April 1, 2029; October 1, 2030; October 1, 2032 on a October 1, 2025 commencement). Force majeure extensions are capped at 12 months in the aggregate, plus 6 months for permitting, for 18 months total. The Bayside loan is for 48 months with two 6-month extensions (60 months maximum). Coventry's completion guaranty to Bayside guarantees "lien-free completion of the Project... on or before the Initial Maturity Date."

*Analysis.* Read together, four schedule problems appear:

> (i) **Zero cushion at Milestone 3.** The final extended loan maturity (60 months) and the Milestone 3 deadline (60 months) are the same day. A project that is one month late is simultaneously in milestone default and past loan maturity.
>
> (ii) **The completion guaranty is 12–30 months tighter than the lease.** Coventry guarantees completion by month 48; the lease permits Phase 1 as late as month 60, and with the 18-month force majeure and permitting allowance, as late as month 78 (April 1, 2032).
>
> (iii) **Phase 2 is outside the loan term.** Milestone 4 (October 1, 2032) is 24 months after the last possible loan maturity; the office building therefore depends on a refinancing or on separate capitalization that is not in the record.
>
> (iv) **Entitlement risk is compressed into Milestone 1.** Construction must commence within 18 months, which requires site plan approval, zoning approvals, coastal and wetlands approvals, building permits, and DEEP approvals for the RAP and Soil Management Plan — with the ELUR ambiguity unresolved and a litigable affordable housing covenant. The ESA also documents a November 2024 nor'easter that put water at approximately 10.5 feet NAVD88 at the bulkhead, and recommends calibrating force majeure provisions to coastal storm risk. The Term Sheet's force majeure list ("acts of God, war, terrorism, civil unrest, strikes, labor disputes, governmental orders or moratoria, pandemics, epidemics, and similar events") does not mention named storms, tidal flooding, storm surge, supply chain disruption (which you specifically raised), or Landlord-caused delay.

*Position taken.* Section 7.4 expands the force majeure list (named storms, tidal flooding and storm surge, FEMA map changes, shortages and supply chain disruption, utility delays, unknown site conditions) and requires only that notice affect the extension by the days of delay in giving it. Section 7.2(c) adds day-for-day extensions for delays attributable to the ELUR, Landlord's title, or the City, outside the 18-month caps. Section 7.2(d) adds a no-penalty termination right if Phase 1 approvals are finally denied. Section 7.5 removes any consequence for a milestone achieved within the cure period. Section 18.9 makes time of the essence for rent and for the closing conditions, but not for the Milestones.

*Fallback.* If the Authority will not expand force majeure, seek a single additional 6-month extension available on written notice without a showing of cause. Separately, and as a matter of internal project management, consider re-basing the loan extension conditions and the Coventry guaranty trigger so that the guarantor's obligation is tied to the lease milestones rather than the initial maturity.

### Issue 12 — Security Deposit: The Step-Down Is Undefined and the Draw Standard Is Loose

**Severity: Medium-High. Sources: Term Sheet Section 8; Instructions Section 5; Bayside Term Sheet Section 4; Resolution (recital).**

*Record facts.* The deposit is $5,700,000 (24 months of initial Base Rent), reducible to $2,850,000 (12 months) "upon Tenant's demonstration to Landlord's reasonable satisfaction that the Project has achieved and maintained an overall occupancy rate of ninety percent (90%) or greater for a period of twenty-four (24) consecutive months." Landlord may draw "upon the occurrence of any uncured Event of Default." The Resolution recital describes a letter of credit "issued by a federally chartered banking institution"; the Term Sheet requires a bank "organized under the laws of the United States or any state thereof" with an A-/A3 rating; Bayside permits a cash deposit at Borrower's option.

*Analysis.* "Overall occupancy rate" is undefined for a mixed-use project with residential, office, and retail components; there is no specification of physical versus economic occupancy, no measurement date, no certification standard, no objection period, no deemed-approval mechanism, and no timetable for the reduction after the condition is met — four separate sources of dispute, exactly as you anticipated. The draw standard ("any uncured Event of Default") would allow a draw for a non-monetary default and for claimed damages, without an accounting. The three form-of-instrument formulations conflict.

*Position taken.* Section 8.3 defines "Occupancy Rate" as leased-and-occupied rentable square footage over delivered and available rentable square footage, requires a chief financial officer's certificate with a rent roll, imposes a 10-Business-Day objection period with deemed approval, references the Expert for disputes, and makes the reduction a one-time, non-revocable reduction with a 10-Business-Day implementation deadline. Section 8.4 limits draws to monetary obligations then due or documented direct damages, requires 10 Business Days' notice to Tenant and each Leasehold Mortgagee, bars draws on good-faith-disputed amounts and on amounts the mortgagee has cured, and requires an accounting and repayment of improper draws with interest. Section 8.2 expressly permits state-chartered banks and a cash alternative. Section 8.5 defers replenishment of disputed amounts.

*Fallback.* If the Authority insists on "reasonable satisfaction," at least fix the objective inputs (rent roll plus certification) and a 15-Business-Day deemed-approval period; without a deemed-approval mechanic the step-down will not be operationally achievable.

### Issue 13 — Definitional Defect: "Lease Year" Means Two Different Things

**Severity: Medium (but pervasive). Sources: Term Sheet Sections 3 and 5.**

*Record facts.* Term Sheet Section 3 measures the 99-year Term and the Lease Expiration Date from the Lease Commencement Date, and Section 5 states that "the first day of Lease Year 1 (which shall be the Rent Commencement Date)" is when escalation begins. Section 6 begins percentage rent in "Lease Year 6"; Section 10 commences the tax abatement on the Lease Commencement Date; Section 9 measures milestones from the Lease Commencement Date.

*Analysis.* One defined term is used on two different clocks, three years apart. Left uncorrected, "Lease Year 6" for percentage rent could mean October 1, 2030 (three years earlier than intended) or October 1, 2033; the tax abatement "Years 1 through 5" could mean 2025–2030 or 2028–2033; and the CPI resets could occur three years early. Across a 99-year instrument, this single ambiguity affects every economic term in the lease.

*Position taken.* The Draft Lease does not use "Lease Year." Section 1.1 defines "Term Year" (from the Lease Commencement Date) and "Rent Year" (from the Rent Commencement Date), with a drafting note explaining the substitution, and each Article specifies which applies. Base Rent escalation, CPI resets, and percentage rent run on Rent Years; the Term, the Milestones, and the abatement period run on Term Years or their own defined periods.

*Fallback.* If Landlord's counsel will not accept the substitution, retain "Lease Year" but define it distinctly for each Article (e.g., "Lease Year (Rent)" and "Lease Year (Term)"). Do not leave the Term Sheet formulation in place.

## VI. LEGAL RESEARCH NOTE — RELIEF FROM THE REVERTER

**The question.** You asked whether Connecticut law provides relief against a forfeiture of improvements grossly disproportionate to the landlord's harm, and whether a principle from a prior Stamford matter applies.

**Preliminary view, subject to verification.** Connecticut applies the conventional liquidated-damages-versus-penalty analysis: a stipulated remedy will be enforced if, at the time of contracting, the harm from breach was difficult to estimate and the stipulated amount was a reasonable forecast of that harm; if the amount is unreasonably large in light of anticipated or actual loss, it is treated as a penalty and is unenforceable. We believe the leading Connecticut authority to be *Nor'easter Group, Inc. v. Colossale Concrete, Inc.*, 207 Conn. 468 (1988), but we have not yet pulled the opinion and you should treat that citation as a lead rather than a conclusion. The Restatement provisions most likely to be useful are Section 356 (liquidated damages and penalties), Section 229 (excuse of a condition to avoid disproportionate forfeiture), and Section 208 (unconscionability); each is persuasive in Connecticut but not binding, and we would need to confirm how the Superior Court has applied them to lease forfeitures. Restatement (Second) of Property (Landlord and Tenant) Section 13.2 (relief from forfeiture) is a further possible source, again as persuasion rather than authority.

**On the Stamford recollection.** We have not located any authority in the record, or in preliminary research, connecting a Stamford project to a disproportionate-forfeiture holding, and we do not recommend relying on a recollection we cannot verify. If you can identify the transaction or the decision, we will check it. Our working hypothesis is that the principle you recall is the penalty doctrine described above, or the Restatement's disproportionate-forfeiture rule, rather than a distinct leasing decision.

**Why the legal argument should not be the plan.** Three reasons. First, a court asked to enforce an express, negotiated reverter in a 99-year ground lease with sophisticated parties may well enforce it: freedom of contract is a strong default, and the forfeiture is not of a statutory or procedural right but of improvements a party agreed to build subject to a stated risk. Second, litigation is a remedy after the loss, and you would be litigating over an asset the Authority then holds. Third, and dispositive commercially, the objection is not only legal but underwriting: Bayside will not close on a lease that permits its collateral to be extinguished without compensation, so the provision must be fixed in negotiation regardless of how a Connecticut court might later rule (Issue 3).

**What the record does support.** The strongest negotiating materials are factual rather than legal: (a) the deposit already secures performance, so the Authority is not without a remedy; (b) the Authority's actual damages from a delay are quantifiable and modest — no Base Rent is payable before the Rent Commencement Date, so a missed Milestone 3 costs months of ground rent, not hundreds of millions; (c) the ratio between the forfeiture (roughly $211–264 million of Phase 1 improvements, plus $5.7 million) and the harm is on the order of a thousand to one; and (d) the Authority's own Resolution requires reverter rights but does not require that they be uncompensated.

**Two further points to verify with Connecticut counsel.** First, whether a redevelopment authority leasing public land for 99 years may enforce a forfeiture of a lessee's improvements, and whether any statutory or public-purpose limitation constrains it. Second, whether the enabling legislation for a disposition of this duration requires municipal legislative approval beyond the Authority's own board action; the record contains the Board's resolution but no City Council action, and the Resolution relies on counsel's advice rather than identifying the statutory grant (Issue 11 of the log).

### Issue 13 — Definitional Defect: "Lease Year" Means Two Different Things

**Severity: Medium (but pervasive). Sources: Term Sheet Sections 3 and 5.**

*Record facts.* Term Sheet Section 3 measures the 99-year Term and the Lease Expiration Date from the Lease Commencement Date, and Section 5 states that "the first day of Lease Year 1 (which shall be the Rent Commencement Date)" is when escalation begins. Section 6 begins percentage rent in "Lease Year 6"; Section 10 commences the tax abatement on the Lease Commencement Date; Section 9 measures milestones from the Lease Commencement Date.

*Analysis.* One defined term is used on two different clocks, three years apart. Left uncorrected, "Lease Year 6" for percentage rent could mean October 1, 2030 (three years earlier than intended) or October 1, 2033; the tax abatement "Years 1 through 5" could mean 2025–2030 or 2028–2033; and the CPI resets could occur three years early. Across a 99-year instrument, this single ambiguity affects every economic term in the lease.

*Position taken.* The Draft Lease does not use "Lease Year." Section 1.1 defines "Term Year" (from the Lease Commencement Date) and "Rent Year" (from the Rent Commencement Date), with a drafting note explaining the substitution, and each Article specifies which applies. Base Rent escalation, CPI resets, and percentage rent run on Rent Years; the Term, the Milestones, and the abatement period run on Term Years or their own defined periods.

*Fallback.* If Landlord's counsel will not accept the substitution, retain "Lease Year" but define it distinctly for each Article (e.g., "Lease Year (Rent)" and "Lease Year (Term)"). Do not leave the Term Sheet formulation in place.

## VI. LEGAL RESEARCH NOTE — RELIEF FROM THE REVERTER

**The question.** You asked whether Connecticut law provides relief against a forfeiture of improvements grossly disproportionate to the landlord's harm, and whether a principle from a prior Stamford matter applies.

**Preliminary view, subject to verification.** Connecticut applies the conventional liquidated-damages-versus-penalty analysis: a stipulated remedy will be enforced if, at the time of contracting, the harm from breach was difficult to estimate and the stipulated amount was a reasonable forecast of that harm; if the amount is unreasonably large in light of anticipated or actual loss, it is treated as a penalty and is unenforceable. We believe the leading Connecticut authority to be *Nor'easter Group, Inc. v. Colossale Concrete, Inc.*, 207 Conn. 468 (1988), but we have not yet pulled the opinion and you should treat that citation as a lead rather than a conclusion. The Restatement provisions most likely to be useful are Section 356 (liquidated damages and penalties), Section 229 (excuse of a condition to avoid disproportionate forfeiture), and Section 208 (unconscionability); each is persuasive in Connecticut but not binding, and we would need to confirm how the Superior Court has applied them to lease forfeitures. Restatement (Second) of Property (Landlord and Tenant) Section 13.2 (relief from forfeiture) is a further possible source, again as persuasion rather than authority.

**On the Stamford recollection.** We have not located any authority in the record, or in preliminary research, connecting a Stamford project to a disproportionate-forfeiture holding, and we do not recommend relying on a recollection we cannot verify. If you can identify the transaction or the decision, we will check it. Our working hypothesis is that the principle you recall is the penalty doctrine described above, or the Restatement's disproportionate-forfeiture rule, rather than a distinct leasing decision.

**Why the legal argument should not be the plan.** Three reasons. First, a court asked to enforce an express, negotiated reverter in a 99-year ground lease with sophisticated parties may well enforce it: freedom of contract is a strong default, and the forfeiture is not of a statutory or procedural right but of improvements a party agreed to build subject to a stated risk. Second, litigation is a remedy after the loss, and you would be litigating over an asset the Authority then holds. Third, and dispositive commercially, the objection is not only legal but underwriting: Bayside will not close on a lease that permits its collateral to be extinguished without compensation, so the provision must be fixed in negotiation regardless of how a Connecticut court might later rule (Issue 3).

**What the record does support.** The strongest negotiating materials are factual rather than legal: (a) the deposit already secures performance, so the Authority is not without a remedy; (b) the Authority's actual damages from a delay are quantifiable and modest — no Base Rent is payable before the Rent Commencement Date, so a missed Milestone 3 costs months of ground rent, not hundreds of millions; (c) the ratio between the forfeiture (roughly $211–264 million of Phase 1 improvements, plus $5.7 million) and the harm is on the order of a thousand to one; and (d) the Authority's own Resolution requires reverter rights but does not require that they be uncompensated.

**Two further points to verify with Connecticut counsel.** First, whether a redevelopment authority leasing public land for 99 years may enforce a forfeiture of a lessee's improvements, and whether any statutory or public-purpose limitation constrains it. Second, whether the enabling legislation for a disposition of this duration requires municipal legislative approval beyond the Authority's own board action; the record contains the Board's resolution but no City Council action, and the Resolution relies on counsel's advice rather than identifying the statutory grant (Issue 11 of the log).
MDEOF

VI. LEGAL RESEARCH NOTE — RELIEF FROM THE REVERTER
The question. You asked whether Connecticut law provides relief against a
forfeiture of improvements grossly disproportionate to the landlord’s harm, and
whether a principle from a prior Stamford matter applies.
Preliminary view, subject to verification. Connecticut applies the conventional
liquidated-damages-versus-penalty analysis: a stipulated remedy will be enforced
if, at the time of contracting, the harm from breach was difficult to estimate and
the stipulated amount was a reasonable forecast of that harm; if the amount is
unreasonably large in light of anticipated or actual loss, it is treated as a penalty
and is unenforceable. We believe the leading Connecticut authority to be
Nor’easter Group, Inc. v. Colossale Concrete, Inc., 207 Conn. 468 (1988), but we
have not yet pulled the opinion and you should treat that citation as a lead rather
than a conclusion. The Restatement provisions most likely to be useful are Section
356 (liquidated damages and penalties), Section 229 (excuse of a condition to
avoid disproportionate forfeiture), and Section 208 (unconscionability); each is
persuasive in Connecticut but not binding, and we would need to confirm how the
Superior Court has applied them to lease forfeitures. Restatement (Second) of
Property (Landlord and Tenant) Section 13.2 (relief from forfeiture) is a further
possible source, again as persuasion rather than authority.
On the Stamford recollection. We have not located any authority in the record,
or in preliminary research, connecting a Stamford project to a disproportionate-
forfeiture holding, and we do not recommend relying on a recollection we cannot
verify. If you can identify the transaction or the decision, we will check it. Our

| File | Description |

| `ground-lease-agreement.docx` | First-draft Ground Lease Agreement (Tenant side), 18 articles, 9 exhibits, ~74 pages |

Both files were validated with the docx validation gate (ZIP integrity, XML well-formedness, relationship consistency) and rendered to PDF for layout review.

# Source record used

Seven documents: client instructions email (6/15/2025); executed Term Sheet (6/10/2025); Bayside construction loan term sheet (5/28/2025); Title Commitment TC-2025-07821 (effective 6/1/2025); Phase II ESA executive summary (5/2/2025); ALTA/NSPS Survey CLS-2025-0417 (4/28/2025); Board Resolution 2025-047 (6/5/2025).

# What the lease does

Built from the Term Sheet's business terms but drafted to be financeable and to protect the leasehold:

- **Reverter repriced** (Art. 7): no automatic termination; 180-day Tenant cure plus an independent 180-day Leasehold Mortgagee cure; Reverter Compensation = greater of appraised FMV or Net Hard Costs, net of Landlord Damages capped at 24 months' Base Rent, with mitigation duty, escrow/no-possession until paid, rescission right, and a limited draw on the security deposit.
- **Lender protections** (Art. 10) drafted to Bayside's Section 5 checklist rather than the Term Sheet summary: no-consent leasehold mortgage, simultaneous notices, independent cure periods, New Lease on *any* termination (30-day execution, equal priority, sublease recognition, improvements included), no surrender/amendment without consent, foreclosure/deed-in-lieu without consent, SNDA, bankruptcy/§365.
- **Percentage rent** (Art. 4): Breakpoint indexed in lockstep with Base Rent; cash-basis Gross Revenues with 17 closed-list exclusions; audit lookback and deemed acceptance.
- **Tax abatement** (Art. 6): runs from Rent Commencement; recorded City agreement as a closing condition; dollar-for-dollar Base Rent offset and termination right on shortfall.
- **Definitional fix**: "Lease Year" replaced with distinct "Term Year" / "Rent Year" to resolve the Term Sheet's three-year ambiguity.
- Also: ELUR ground-floor program and DEEP process (Art. 5, 9.3), remediation cost bands and credit acceleration/cash-out, mechanics' lien as a Landlord obligation (not a Permitted Exception), recorded ROFR amendment with eight carve-outs, objective LOC step-down with deemed approval, casualty/condemnation valuation mechanics, tenant-favourable default remedies, and Term Sheet supersession.

# Key findings the memo surfaces (beyond the client's own list)

1. **Title Commitment Exhibit A is arithmetically false** — its own courses (580.00 ft × 480.00 ft) enclose ~279,535 SF (6.42 acres) against a stated 139,392 SF, and describe a different surveyor/drawing than the Survey in the file (435.22 ft × 320.47 ft).
2. **Bulkhead** stated at ~480 LF in four documents but the surveyed eastern boundary is 320.47 ft; pedestrian easement area computed on the 480-ft assumption (7,200 SF vs 4,807 SF); structure described inconsistently (concrete/timber vs steel sheet pile); no cost allocated anywhere in the record.
3. **Recorded 2019 ROFR has no mortgage/foreclosure carve-out** and reaches "any interest" in the leasehold — a direct conflict with Bayside §§5.1 and 5.6 that only a recorded amendment can cure.
4. **Tax abatement is not binding on the tax levying entity**; worth ~$46.4M nominal over 15 years, of which ~$4.6M is lost by starting the clock at Lease Commencement rather than Rent Commencement.
5. **Percentage rent with a fixed Breakpoint** runs from ~0.9% to ~30% of Base Rent by Year 99 (~$146M more than an indexed construct on an illustrative revenue path).
6. **ESA contingency is mislabelled**: the "10%" lines are 5.71% and 4.76%, understating the estimate by $102,500 before the excluded RAP, SMP, DEEP fees, verification, dewatering, and bulkhead costs.
7. **Schedule conflict**: Milestone 3 coincides exactly with Bayside's final extended maturity; Coventry's completion guaranty runs to month 48; Phase 2 (2032) falls outside the loan term.
8. Plus: mechanics' lien treated as a Permitted Exception though Title Requirement No. 7 bars policy issuance; three conflicting AMI geographies; blank/unexecuted Resolution certification; City not a party to the abatement; no Landlord environmental indemnity; unexecuted Bayside term sheet that expired 6/27/2025.

# Points requiring client instruction

Part VII of the memo lists 16 deliberate departures from the Term Sheet (5 of which likely require a supplemental Board resolution) and asks for two decisions: the "greater of" reverter measure, and appetite for the $4.5M remediation walk-away. Part VIII lists 16 information requests keyed to owners and dates.
"}

{"summary": "Drafted a tenant-side ground lease and a companion issues memorandum from the seven-document record (client instructions, executed Term Sheet, Bayside construction loan term sheet, Title Commitment TC-2025-07821, Phase II ESA summary, ALTA/NSPS Survey, and Board Resolution 2025-047).

**ground-lease-agreement.docx** (~74 pages, 18 articles, 9 exhibits) implements the Term Sheet economics with tenant protections and Bayside's Section 5 lender requirements: a repriced reverter (no automatic termination; independent 180-day mortgagee cure; compensation equal to the greater of appraised FMV or Net Hard Costs, net of Landlord Damages capped at 24 months' rent, with escrow/no-possession-until-paid and a limited deposit draw); full Article 10 leasehold-mortgage package (no-consent mortgage, notices, cure rights, New Lease on any termination, no amendment/surrender without consent, foreclosure and deed-in-lieu without consent, SNDA, §365); percentage rent with a Breakpoint indexed in lockstep with Base Rent and a closed list of 17 exclusions from cash-basis Gross Revenues; a tax abatement running from Rent Commencement and backed by a recorded City agreement, rent offset and termination right; ELUR/DEEP process protections; remediation cost bands and credit acceleration; the mechanics' lien as a Landlord obligation rather than a Permitted Exception; a required amendment to the recorded ROFR with eight carve-outs; an objective, deemed-approval LOC step-down; and separate "Term Year"/"Rent Year" definitions to cure the Term Sheet's three-year ambiguity.

**drafting-issues-memo.docx** (~31 pages) opens with a risk-prioritised top-ten register, then analyses 13 priority issues (facts/sources, analysis, position taken, fallback, open item), and adds a 55-item issue log, a 40-line numerical reconciliation schedule, a hedged Connecticut legal research note on penalty/disproportionate forfeiture (with the unverified "Stamford" recollection flagged as needing the client's identification), a table of 16 deliberate departures from the Term Sheet and their Board-approval implications, and 16 dated information requests.

Notable independent findings: the Title Commitment's Exhibit A courses enclose ~279,535 SF (6.42 acres) against a stated 139,392 SF and describe a different surveyor and drawing than the Survey on file; the bulkhead is stated at ~480 LF against a 320.47-ft surveyed boundary and is described inconsistently and costed nowhere; the recorded 2019 ROFR has no mortgage or foreclosure carve-out; the ESA's "10%" contingency lines are actually 5.71% and 4.76% (understating remediation by $102,500 before excluded items); Milestone 3 coincides exactly with Bayside's final extended maturity while Coventry's completion guaranty runs to month 48; and the abatement is worth ~$46.4M nominal, of which ~$4.6M is lost by starting the clock at Lease Commencement.

Both deliverables pass the docx validation gate and were rendered to PDF for layout review.", "deliverables": ["ground-lease-agreement.docx", "drafting-issues-memo.docx", "response.md"]}
